title: fix(dspy): find dspy's distribution by the package it installs
body:
## Problem

The 3.5.0 release workflow failed in `build-and-publish-test-pypi` ([run](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/actions/runs/42849991537/job/129947794494)): 7 `LocalInterpreter` RLM tests in `tests/predict/test_rlm.py` saw `dspy.Image` arrive in the REPL as a `dict`. Because that job gates PyPI, nothing was published.

## Root cause

`sandbox_bundle._distributions()` started from `_detect_dspy_dist()`, which only knows the names `dspy` and `dspy-ai`. The TestPyPI job installs the wheel as `dspy-ai-test-isaac`, so the lookup found nothing, `sandbox_modules()` was empty, and `facade._in_sandbox("dspy.…")` returned `False`. The host then sent dspy's own types as plain data instead of as their class. The same breakage hits any install under another name, such as a fork. Main CI and the real PyPI job install as `dspy`, so they passed. A leftover `dspy.egg-info` in a checkout also hides the bug.

## Fix

Find the distribution that actually provides the `dspy` package with `importlib.metadata.packages_distributions()`, and fall back to the existing name lookup.

## Verification

- New regression test in `tests/primitives/test_facade.py`: dspy installed only under another distribution name still encodes `dspy.Image` as its class. It fails without the fix (`None == 'dspy.adapters.types.image.Image'`) and passes with it.
- Reproduced the release job locally: I built the renamed wheel with `python -m build` on Python 3.11.18 and installed it into a fresh venv in a clean checkout. Before the fix: the same 7 failures, 720 passed. After: `pytest tests/metadata/test_metadata.py tests/predict` gives 727 passed, 223 skipped.
- `tests/primitives tests/predict tests/flex tests/utils`: 1171 passed, 477 skipped. `ruff check` is clean.

After this merges, the release needs a re-tag on the fixed commit (or 3.5.1).

title: fix(clients): exclude LiteLLM releases with eager MCP imports
body:
## Problem and root cause

Ordinary optional-LiteLLM inference can fail before HTTP with missing `mcp` / `CacheableResult`. DSPy's default OpenAI route now selects Responses, exposing this on unchanged constructors that used Chat in 3.4.1. A same-dependency-graph public Predict comparison confirms that transition; native inference is unaffected.

LiteLLM 1.106.0–1.106.7 and 1.108.0–1.108.3 eagerly import proxy MCP handler → catalog → MCP-2-only `CacheableResult`, even without gateway tools. Plain Chat avoids it, but ordinary Chat function tools also trigger it. All twelve stable releases were source-audited; adjacent 1.105.7 is clean and 1.108.4 fixes both dispatch paths ([upstream #45961](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/pull/45961)).

## Compatibility boundary

- Exclude those twelve releases, retaining the existing >=1.65.8 floor and older working versions.
- Lock LiteLLM 1.108.4; retain MCP 1.29.0. No native/runtime inference changes or forced MCP-major upgrade.
- **Conservative tradeoff:** dependency metadata cannot condition one distribution's version on another installed distribution. The exclusions therefore also reject affected LiteLLM versions with MCP 2 where ordinary inference passes. This is not certification of every otherwise eligible release. Actual gateway users still need LiteLLM's own version-specific MCP extra.

## Proof

- 25 isolated fixed-shared-dependency environments: 50 real-SDK loopback Chat/Responses cases plus 10 async/function controls; credentials cleared, nonlocal sockets blocked, no paid calls for dependency work.
- Built-wheel resolver rejects all twelve exclusions; accepts 1.65.8, 1.96.0, 1.105.7 and 1.108.4. Base/optional/independent-MCP-1 install paths checked.
- New regression cases cover sync/async × default/Chat/Responses × ordinary/function-tool calls. Isolated local profiles: **38 passed** with MCP absent; **38 passed** with MCP 1.29.0, including Python 3.12 validation and fresh reruns after the workflow removal.
- Broad optional suite: **1427 passed, 21 skipped**; native suite: **1383 passed, 65 skipped**; fresh optional-free installed wheel: **6 passed**.
- Lock consistency, Ruff, `ty check`, and diff whitespace checks pass. Independent review completed. Per maintainer direction, **no workflow changes**: optional profiles are local evidence, not new CI jobs. Optional-client tests skip when LiteLLM is not installed.

Source audit and bounded live-campaign evidence: [consolidated report](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/dspy-3-5-independent-live-regression-and-compatibility-resul-54641304-4f76-4502-9ae4-b89f771a5b1f). Actual MCP sessions, every provider/version, and prerelease/postrelease boundaries are not certified.

title: fix(adapters): preserve nested XML enum and null guidance
body:
## Fix

Nested XML output templates dropped enum/const constraints to `...`, leaving models to guess valid values. Preserve those constraints (including referenced enums and falsy constants), and replace literal `<field/>` null guidance with “self-close the field's own tag.”

Two files, +34/−3. No parser changes. **No public API signature changes.**

## Evidence

- On current `main`, four prompt regression checks fail without the fix; with it, `pytest -q tests/adapters tests/streaming`: **771 passed, 3 skipped**. Pre-commit/type checks pass.

| Model / provider | Exact old → new | Typed parse old → new |
|---|---|---|
| Haiku 4.5 / Azure | 5/6 → 6/6 | 5/6 → 6/6 |
| Qwen3.8 2.4T A95B / OpenRouter→Alibaba | 5/6 → 5/6 | 5/6 → 6/6 |
| Kimi K3 / OpenRouter→Moonshot AI | 5/6 → 5/6 | 6/6 → 6/6 |

The observed enum benefit is narrow: Haiku/Qwen emitted `Shipment` for `Literal["shipment"]`; the new template supplied the required lowercase value. This small cohort does not establish general non-regression. Earlier provider-rejected attempts are retained separately, not adapter failures.

title: fix(cache): handle restricted disk entries consistently
body:
### Problem

`restrict_pickle=True` applied its decoder to cached values, but non-raw keys still used diskcache's default loader and file-backed entries used row filenames directly during reads and cleanup. Array values relied on pickle reconstruction. A cache directory with malformed rows could therefore behave differently depending on which field or operation was reached; dictionaries containing arrays also need to remain cacheable across processes.

### Change

The restricted disk checks resolved class identities, uses the same decoder for pickled keys, validates file-backed names, and uses handle-relative file operations on POSIX for reads, writes, and cleanup. Plain NumPy arrays use data-only `.npy` bytes; arrays inside containers use the same bytes through a tagged pickle reference. Entries without arrays retain their on-disk format, and `restrict_pickle=False` still uses diskcache's original disk.

### Proof

The disk-only DSPy cache round-trips a nested array through the public API. A retained test also reopens the cache and checks the result:

```python
import numpy as np
import dspy

dspy.configure_cache(enable_disk_cache=True, enable_memory_cache=False,
                     disk_cache_dir=cache_dir, restrict_pickle=True)
request = {"model": "test", "prompt": "embedding"}
value = {"embedding": np.arange(6, dtype=np.float32)}
dspy.cache.put(request, value)
np.testing.assert_array_equal(dspy.cache.get(request)["embedding"], value["embedding"])
```

Focused regressions failed on their respective pre-fix heads and pass here. Local cache and LM-boundary tests: **109 passed**; locked type check, Ruff, and whitespace checks pass. No provider calls.

### Limits

Older pickled arrays become cache misses and are recomputed; NumPy object arrays and subclasses are not persisted in restricted mode. On Windows, pathname validation remains best effort against concurrent directory replacement. The POSIX file operations use directory descriptors and no-follow flags.

title: Default LM API-family selection to native lm15 routing
body:
## Summary

Make `dspy.LM(..., model_type="auto")` the default, using lm15's existing native API-family routing before capability planning/request shaping. This is separate from `engine="auto"` (native vs optional LiteLLM). No model-name exceptions, new transport, error-triggered API replay, or reasoning downgrade.

- OpenAI/Azure use Responses; Anthropic/Gemini/OpenRouter keep native dialects. Registrations and custom engines retain ownership. Unknown compatibility routes stay Chat.
- Preserve explicit chat/responses/text, saved explicit-chat states, string-list default returns, typed returns, copy/cache identity, and family selection through compatibility fallback. Refuse unmapped native Responses fallbacks locally rather than invent a LiteLLM destination.
- Migration: Chat-only models, OpenAI-compatible proxies and Azure deployments must opt into `model_type="chat"` or declare their dialect. Provider routing is not endpoint capability discovery. Existing Chat-wire fixtures now select Chat explicitly.

## Public ReAct request reproduction

```python
import dspy

lm = dspy.LM("openai/gpt-6-luna", max_tokens=2000, cache=False, num_retries=0)
with dspy.context(lm=lm):
    result = dspy.ReAct("question -> answer", tools=[], max_iters=1)(
        question="What is 17 plus 6?"
    )
print(result.answer)
```

Identical socket-guarded first-request capture on base [0cae9e00](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/0cae9e00e1afd02202b1c61ee81693371c40afef) versus this change:

```diff
-POST /v1/chat/completions
-max_completion_tokens: 2000
-reasoning_effort: low
-tools: [{type: function, function: {name: submit, ...}}]
+POST /v1/responses
+max_output_tokens: 2000
+reasoning: {effort: low, summary: auto}
+tools: [{type: function, name: submit, ...}]
```

Synthetic replies prove public ReAct parsing, preserved tools/effort, explicit Chat errors, and no replay. These captures **do not prove live Luna acceptance or resolution of Sol's reported reasoning exhaustion**. [CMP-1785](https://linear.app/cmpnd/issue/CMP-1785) reports SDK Chat failures too; sanitized paired receipts are still needed. Explicit `model_type="responses"` remains the workaround on older DSPy defaults.

## Verification and limits

- New targeted tests against unchanged production: 11 failed / 1 passing control; captures use the same public workload before/after.
- Final credential-cleared/socket-guarded client/adapter/predict/streaming/facade/server suites: **2696 passed, 260 skipped**. Focused suite with minimum LiteLLM 1.65.8: 187 passed, including real SDK Responses against a local HTTP server. Guarded full native-profile run: 3534 passed / 415 skipped; 4 failures + 5 setup errors are external image/PDF fixture downloads denied by the network guard, not suppressed.
- Independent review: no introduced blockers after compatibility corrections. Ruff CI command, `ty check`, and `git diff --check` pass. Default-auto Responses SSE through public streaming prediction/cache is covered alongside explicit Chat.
- Optional-SDK gate: locked/latest LiteLLM 1.106.5/1.108.3 + MCP 1.29.0 fail before Responses HTTP importing `mcp.types.CacheableResult`. Two existing minimum-SDK Responses mock-mode failures also reproduce on pristine base. Neither is hidden or fixed here.
- Safety disclosure: an initial broad run accidentally enabled the existing unmarked `test_usage_tracker_in_parallel` via inherited credentials; GPT-4o-mini appears to have completed. Exact tokens/spend are unknown. Subsequent broad verification clears credentials and blocks non-local sockets, with an offline preflight. The regression lead owns the separate live-opt-in marker fix; it is not included here. No authorized/live Luna/Sol probe was performed.

No merge requested.

title: fix(dspy): read the disk cache through diskcache-community's SafeDisk
body:
## 📝 Changes Description

Closes #10854

`diskcache` 5.6.3 is unmaintained (last release August 2023) and flagged by scanners with no fixed version, and it is a required dependency, so every dspy install carries the finding. This keeps persistent caching and the `restrict_pickle` and `safe_types` API, and moves the cache onto a maintained package that does the restricted reading itself.

This MR/PR contains the following changes:

- **Dependency.** Depend on `diskcache-community>=5.8.4` instead of `diskcache`. It is a maintained, faster fork with the same API, the same files on disk as diskcache 5.6.3 and the same license (Apache-2.0). `uv.lock` changes only for this package.
- **Disk.** `restricted_disk` now returns `SafeDisk.with_types(*safe_types, modules=("openai.types",)).with_numpy().with_options(on_error="miss")`, and dspy's own unpickler is removed. `SafeDisk` reads keys and values through an allowlist, checks values before writing them, and keeps file paths inside the cache directory.
- **Miss on error.** A refused or corrupt entry is deleted and treated as a miss by the disk, so the `DeserializationError` handling in `Cache.get` goes away; the name stays as an alias of `pickle.UnpicklingError`. `Cache.get` still never raises on an entry it cannot read: a missing package or a `MemoryError` / `RecursionError` while reading is a miss, as before.
- **Arrays.** `SafeDisk.with_numpy()` stores arrays in the fork's validated array format, so ndarray caching behaves exactly as it does today, including a callable `Embedder` and the existing `test_callable_numpy_embedding_persists_to_disk`. numpy stays optional: nothing imports it unless a value needs it.
- **Docs.** Updated the "Restricting Pickle Deserialization" section of the cache tutorial.

`restrict_pickle=False` still uses the plain `Disk`, unchanged.

### How this was tested

- `pytest -m 'not extra and not deno' tests/`: 3536 passed, 361 skipped, 304 deselected and 2 xfailed on Python 3.12.
- `ty check` passes. `ruff check` reports only the C408 in `cache.py` that `main` already has (same unchanged line).
- The cache, serialization and embedding tests pass, including `test_callable_numpy_embedding_persists_to_disk` and the two fresh-process round-trip tests.
- The six planted-row cases from the issue, each against a real `dspy.clients.cache.Cache` with one column of one row rewritten in `cache.db`, run on this commit (`844c9fbda`) with diskcache-community 5.8.4:
  1. **Case 1: a stored value that runs a command directly.**
     - **On main:** blocked, the entry is refused and treated as a miss.
     - **On this branch:** reads as a miss; no command runs.
  2. **Case 2: a stored value that runs a command through a name dspy trusts.**
     - **On main:** the command runs when the entry is read.
     - **On this branch:** reads as a miss; no command runs.
  3. **Case 3: the same command, stored in the key instead of the value.**
     - **On main:** the command runs the first time anything lists the cache.
     - **On this branch:** iterates zero keys; no command runs.
  4. **Case 4: a numpy array with forged internals.**
     - **On main:** the process dies (SIGSEGV, exit -11).
     - **On this branch:** reads as a miss instead of terminating the process.
  5. **Case 5: an entry that points at a file outside the cache, then is deleted.**
     - **On main:** the outside file is deleted.
     - **On this branch:** the outside file is kept; `delete` raises `ValueError`.
  6. **Case 6: the same as case 5, triggered by routine cleanup.**
     - **On main:** the outside file is deleted.
     - **On this branch:** the outside file is kept; 200/200 ordinary writes after the tamper are stored and readable.

<details>
<summary>Raw output: fix branch (844c9fbda, diskcache-community 5.8.4)</summary>

```
direct-value   exit=0      get returned type NoneType | marker created: False
dotted-value   exit=0      get returned type NoneType | marker created: False
key-row        exit=0      iteration returned 0 keys | marker created: False
numpy-value    exit=0      get returned type NoneType | marker created: False
path-delete    exit=0      delete raised ValueError | outside file still there: True
path-cull      exit=0      outside file still there: True | later writes stored and readable: 200/200
```

</details>

Tests in `test_disk_serialization.py` that expected `DeserializationError` or a pickled ndarray refusal are rewritten for the new behaviour. `test_ndarray_roundtrip` and `test_numpy_ctypeslib_blocked` are kept; added `test_numpy_cannot_be_registered_as_safe_type`. In `test_cache.py`, `test_corrupt_disk_entries_return_none` is kept and `test_tampered_disk_entry_is_a_cache_miss` covers a planted entry reading as a miss.

Moving a cache directory between versions:

| Step | Plain records and SDK responses | Arrays |
|---|---|---|
| Written by `main`, read by this branch | Read back unchanged | Miss once, then a hit |
| Written by this branch, read by `main` | Read back unchanged | Miss, computed again |

Not run: `extra`, `deno` and `llm_call` tests, and Python 3.10, 3.13, 3.14 and 3.15. These are left to CI.

## ✅ Contributor Checklist

title: fix: preserve JSON nulls in Deno tool results
body:
## JSON null reaches sandboxed Python as the wrong value

Structured host-tool results, including results from the host adapter serving a sandboxed predictor, pass through Deno/Pyodide. Before this fix, JavaScript `JSON.parse` followed by `JsProxy.to_py` turns JSON null into Pyodide's `JsNull`, **not Python None**. The real-DSPy sandbox can then serialize that object as the string `"jsnull"`.

An order-support workflow looks up two orders and prepares a follow-up queue. The first order has not shipped and its customer has no email on file. The JSON order-service response contains null for both `tracking_number` and nested `customer.email`. Guest Python should select “Awaiting carrier assignment” and “Ask customer for email.” Instead it selects **“Track jsnull” and “Email jsnull”** because neither value is Python None.

That customer's literal username is `"jsnull"`; it must remain exactly that string. A second order already has a tracking number and email and must keep them. The complete example below runs this ordinary Python control flow through the real public Local/Deno interpreters with a deterministic order-service tool, not a live API or a model. It shows an incorrect support action, not just an unexpected representation on return to the host.

This is separate from the explicit-default metadata loss in #10843. Restoring a non-null default avoids taking this path, but does not make genuine None survive transport.

## The fix belongs at the JSON-to-Python boundary

Previously, `toolCallBridge` parsed a JSON-valued result into JavaScript data, then the generated Python tool wrapper used `result.to_py()`. That conversion creates `JsNull` inside containers. It is too late to distinguish it reliably once later serialization has turned it into text.

The production diff is **+10/−13 lines in `dspy/primitives/runner.js`**:

- For JSON-valued results, return the existing JSON text across the JS/Pyodide boundary and decode it with Python `json.loads`.
- For string results, JSON-quote the string first. A user string `"null"`, `"jsnull"`, or `"None"` therefore remains a string, rather than being interpreted as a sentinel or JSON syntax.
- JSON-encode the existing response-ID mismatch, host-tool error, and bridge-exception payloads as well. The Python wrapper still recognizes their marker and raises a contextual `RuntimeError`.

```diff
-    parsed = result.to_py() if isinstance(result, JsProxy) else result
+    parsed = json.loads(result)
```

Python's JSON decoder supplies the recursive null-to-None behavior; no recursive cleanup helper, string coercion, signature policy, or new dependency is added. The separate host-side compatibility rule mapping a **raw top-level tool return of None to an empty string is unchanged**. This patch fixes null *inside structured JSON payloads*, which includes predictor outputs.

## Historical implementation proof

The implementation run used baseline production [afaac2646](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b), including GEPA graduation #10796. The after run used the production patch subsequently committed as [d4bea826b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/d4bea826b69acaac15ccbef752b0931f3b7a516d). R5 was not part of either checkout. For the before run, the new tests were present but the production fix was not. These are retained original implementation results, separate from the fresh order-workflow execution below.

```console
$ PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/flex/test_flex_class_signature.py tests/primitives/test_python_interpreter.py -k 'preserves_null_and_string or tool_json_null' --deno -q --tb=short
# Before: baseline production + regression tests
5 failed, 4 passed, 144 deselected in 5.38s
# After: production fix + the same regression cases
9 passed, 144 deselected in 13.24s
```

| Case | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flex: omitted note, explicitly supplied null, literal `jsnull`, or empty string; all also contain a nested null; Local | 4 pass | 4 pass |
| The same four Flex cases; Deno | 4 fail | 4 pass |
| Deno tool result: test null identity inside both a list and a nested dictionary | 1 fail | 1 pass |

The Flex cases explicitly use JSONAdapter, so a supplied JSON null is not confused with the text `"None"` emitted by a text-format fixture. Their expected nested value is `[None, "jsnull", "", "null", "None"]`: blanket replacement of sentinel-looking strings would fail these controls.

The interpreter test evaluates `is None` **inside guest Python**. Its recorded pre-fix result was `[False, "jsnull", False]`, versus expected `[True, "jsnull", True]`. Merely returning a container to the host would be inadequate proof: conversion back through JavaScript JSON can hide the guest's wrong `JsNull` type.

## Complete public workflow: order lookup to support queue

Save this exact example as `test_order_lookup.py`. The tool is an in-memory stand-in for a JSON order-service endpoint. The interpreter runs the batch lookup, null checks, and follow-up selection inside guest Python—the same kind of code an RLM could run in its REPL. No RLM planner or live service is invoked in this deterministic reproduction. The supplied second order, literal username, delivery note, and empty note are compatibility controls, not replacement values derived from the implementation.

```python
import dspy
import pytest


def lookup_order(order_id: str):
    """Deterministic stand-in for a JSON order-service response; no network call."""
    return {
        "SO-1042": {
            "tracking_number": None,
            "customer": {"handle": "jsnull", "email": None},
            "delivery_note": "Leave with reception",
        },
        "SO-1043": {
            "tracking_number": "TRK-8021",
            "customer": {"handle": "riley", "email": "riley@example.com"},
            "delivery_note": "",
        },
    }[order_id]


@pytest.mark.parametrize("factory", [dspy.LocalInterpreter, dspy.PythonInterpreter], ids=["local", "deno"])
def test_order_support_queue(factory):
    # The same ordinary Python branching could be written by an RLM in its REPL.
    code = """
queue = []
for order_id in ["SO-1042", "SO-1043"]:
    order = lookup_order(order_id=order_id)
    tracking = order["tracking_number"]
    email = order["customer"]["email"]
    queue.append({
        "order": order_id,
        "status": "Awaiting carrier assignment" if tracking is None else f"Track {tracking}",
        "contact": "Ask customer for email" if email is None else f"Email {email}",
        "handle": order["customer"]["handle"],
        "delivery_note": order["delivery_note"],
    })
queue
"""
    with factory(tools={"lookup_order": lookup_order}) as interpreter:
        actual = interpreter.execute(code)
    print(f"{factory.__name__}: {actual!r}")
    assert actual == [
        {"order": "SO-1042", "status": "Awaiting carrier assignment", "contact": "Ask customer for email",
         "handle": "jsnull", "delivery_note": "Leave with reception"},
        {"order": "SO-1043", "status": "Track TRK-8021", "contact": "Email riley@example.com",
         "handle": "riley", "delivery_note": ""},
    ]
```

With the target checkout installed, run:

```bash
PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/python -m pytest test_order_lookup.py -q -s --tb=short
```

### Fresh execution of that exact example

The exact code above was executed on detached worktrees at broken [afaac2646](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b) and fixed [d4bea826b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/d4bea826b69acaac15ccbef752b0931f3b7a516d), separately from R5. With development/Deno dependencies already installed, the target checkout was installed editable before each run:

```console
$ uv pip install --python /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python --no-deps -e /tmp/r5-r16-repro-before
# Then, for the fixed run:
$ uv pip install --python /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python --no-deps -e /tmp/r16-repro-fixed
```

The same command ran from each corresponding checkout:

```console
$ PATH="/home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin:$PATH" env -u PYTHONPATH -u OPENAI_API_KEY /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -m pytest /home/user/workspace/repo/.amp/in/artifacts/realistic-sandbox-repros/test_order_lookup.py -q -s --tb=short
# Broken afaac2646:
1 failed, 1 passed in 1.03s
# Fixed d4bea826b:
2 passed in 1.01s
```

Actual Deno stdout before and after:

```text
# Broken:
PythonInterpreter: [{'order': 'SO-1042', 'status': 'Track jsnull', 'contact': 'Email jsnull', 'handle': 'jsnull', 'delivery_note': 'Leave with reception'}, {'order': 'SO-1043', 'status': 'Track TRK-8021', 'contact': 'Email riley@example.com', 'handle': 'riley', 'delivery_note': ''}]
# Fixed:
PythonInterpreter: [{'order': 'SO-1042', 'status': 'Awaiting carrier assignment', 'contact': 'Ask customer for email', 'handle': 'jsnull', 'delivery_note': 'Leave with reception'}, {'order': 'SO-1043', 'status': 'Track TRK-8021', 'contact': 'Email riley@example.com', 'handle': 'riley', 'delivery_note': ''}]
```

LocalInterpreter produced the expected queue before and after. Fresh host, `python -I`, and actual LocalInterpreter-worker checks of `dspy.__file__` all matched `/tmp/r5-r16-repro-before/dspy/__init__.py` before and `/tmp/r16-repro-fixed/dspy/__init__.py` after. **PYTHONPATH alone cannot select the isolated worker's source.** Deno ran rather than being skipped. No live/provider calls were made; initial Deno/Pyodide setup may download dependencies. This example exercises branching on structured null, not the unchanged raw top-level tool None behavior. No repository source or test-suite changes were made for this refresh.

## What the historical predictor-path comparison establishes

The earlier retained Flex probe at `.amp/in/artifacts/r5/deno_none_repro.py` declares an optional output with `default=None`, omits it from a DummyLM response, and returns that nested predictor output through `Flex.load_state`. That identical probe—not the new order-tool workflow above—was run against each installed target in `/tmp/r5-null-main`, using the same dependency environment. The source revision in that disposable checkout was changed and installed editable between runs; it was not selected only with PYTHONPATH.

```console
$ uv pip install --python /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python --no-deps -e /tmp/r5-null-main
$ PATH="/home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin:$PATH" /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -m pytest /home/user/workspace/repo/.amp/in/artifacts/r5/deno_none_repro.py -q --tb=short
```

| Installed source | Recorded output | Interpretation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #10776 parent, [8bdac7c48](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/8bdac7c48edafd49b01c38a633fde1433d9935a8) | `2 passed in 0.88s` | Local and Deno preserve None |
| #10776, [fd1dfc6aa](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/fd1dfc6aa4f05d6773ee2770e665d7d0b01c8f6e) | `1 failed, 1 passed in 8.43s` | Deno returns `"jsnull"`; Local passes |
| #10828 parent, [25f81a83a](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/25f81a83a7a4d32ed7870de7c83602148c744a10) | `1 failed, 1 passed in 8.90s` | Same failure, before that transport merge |
| Unchanged main, [afaac2646](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b) | `1 failed, 1 passed in 9.56s` | Same failure |

After this fix, the same retained probe passed on both backends:

```console
$ PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/artifacts/r5/deno_none_repro.py -q --tb=short
2 passed in 1.51s
```

This establishes that **#10776 introduced/exposed the regression in the public sandboxed-predictor path**. It does not establish that JavaScript/Pyodide's generic null conversion was first introduced in that PR. It also distinguishes the defect from #10828 and from the R5 metadata fix. These historical comparisons were executed during implementation, not repeated for the new order-tool example.

## Historical broader and combined validation

```console
$ PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:/usr/bin:$PATH" env -u OPENAI_API_KEY .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/flex tests/predict/test_rlm.py tests/primitives/test_local_interpreter.py tests/primitives/test_python_interpreter.py tests/primitives/test_sandbox_serializable.py tests/adapters/test_chat_adapter.py tests/adapters/test_xml_adapter.py tests/adapters/test_json_adapter.py tests/adapters/test_reasoning.py --deno -q -n 4 --tb=short
944 passed, 2 skipped, 1 warning in 105.82s (0:01:45)
```

The skips are two live-provider tests, and the warning is an existing TwoStepAdapter deprecation. Existing tests cover raw top-level None, integer/float/bool results, nonserializable and nonfinite-value string fallbacks, tool errors, and recovery. This is focused multi-module coverage, not a full-repository local run.

An isolated checkout then combined exact R16 head [d4bea826b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/d4bea826b69acaac15ccbef752b0931f3b7a516d) with exact R5 head [c74c1879f](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/c74c1879ffb12c6f8de1b056b28d307c3b6aac9c), applied without committing. A separate environment installed that checkout, and host/isolated-worker paths were checked. No combined branch was pushed or merged.

```console
$ PATH="/home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin:$PATH" /tmp/r5-typing-env/bin/python -m pytest tests/flex/test_flex_class_signature.py tests/predict/test_rlm.py tests/primitives/test_python_interpreter.py -k 'preserves_output_defaults or preserves_explicit_output_default or preserves_null_and_string or tool_json_null' --deno -q --tb=short
23 passed, 505 deselected in 22.09s
$ PATH="/home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin:$PATH" /tmp/r5-typing-env/bin/python -m pytest /home/user/workspace/repo/.amp/in/release_3_5_followup.py /home/user/workspace/repo/.amp/in/artifacts/r5/deno_none_repro.py -k 'output_default or explicit_none_transport' -q --tb=short
14 passed, 60 deselected in 7.54s
```

The 23 cases include omitted/provided defaults, explicit None, literal/empty strings, nested values, host reuse of traced predictors, RLM, and Local/Deno. The additional 14 are the original defaults probes plus the retained null probe, not fourteen new distinct behaviors. The temporary combined checkout/environment was removed after validation.

## Review and limits

- An independent bounded review found no blockers and independently ran 17 focused tests. Real-runner probes confirmed response-ID mismatch, closed stdin, and malformed-envelope JSON become catchable contextual guest errors. In the deliberately closed-stdin probe, later host shutdown raised `ValueError` on the manually closed file; guest error propagation had succeeded, and that cleanup behavior was not repaired or counted as a fix here.
- Deno check, internal type checking, CI's Ruff fix check, and whitespace checks passed. At implementation completion, this exact head had **25 successful checks**, only `publish-current` intentionally skipped, and **Greptile 5/5**. [CI runs and detailed logs](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/actions?query=branch%3Afix%2Fdeno-json-null). The realistic-workflow refresh reran only the example above, not CI or the broader suite.
- Raw top-level tool None still maps to an empty string. Arbitrary sandbox default factories and signature-default metadata are outside this fix. No strings are broadly coerced, and no paid or live-provider calls were made by the local validation.
- The overlap inspection during implementation found #10837 changed runner snapshot plumbing, not this decoder; no duplicate fix was found. That inspection was not a claim of an executed integration test with #10837.

AI assistance: Amp in an Isaac-directed release-validation sweep, for reproduction, implementation, testing, independent bounded review, and this description expansion. Prompt scope: “Isolate null transport from default metadata, preserve user strings, prove Local/Deno and nested/provided-output behavior, obtain bounded independent review, and wait for CI/Greptile without merging.”

title: fix(xml): honor positional tuple schemas
body:
## XML drops the schema for each position of a nested tuple

Consider a user extracting wind measurements from field notes into labeled time series for a chart. A Pydantic `WindReport` contains `unit: str` and `stations: list[tuple[str, list[int]]]`; each tuple pairs a station name with its samples in time order. Notes give the north roof's readings as 12, 9, 15 m/s and the south roof's as 4, 7, 5 m/s. The expected station entries are `('north roof', [12, 9, 15])` and `('south roof', [4, 7, 5])`.

Before this fix, valid nested XML reconstructs the north roof's sample position as `{'item': ['12', '9', '15']}` instead of `[12, 9, 15]`, and similarly for the south roof. Public `Predict` raises `AdapterParseError` because both `stations.0.1` and `stations.1.1` must be lists. This is the same supported positional `tuple[str, list[int]]` shape a user reaches by requesting labeled series, not an invented invalid tuple.

Historical tuple probes reproduced the defect with both independently written XML and the adapter's own formatting of a valid typed value. With XML fallback disabled, public `Predict` raised. The original default-adapter probe could recover through JSON, but used **two generations instead of one**; Chat/JSON controls used one. Recovery does not establish correct XML decoding. Historical release investigation also found the opt-in XML defect before XML became the default; the direct repair evidence below is against the named main baseline, not a fresh bisect.

### Task realism and simpler public approaches

The task is to copy station names, units and readings from notes while retaining the three time positions, not infer missing measurements. An LM could plausibly do this; the fixture does not measure its accuracy or likelihood of producing the nested XML. Under the existing positional contract, an ordinary JSON response is `{"report": {"unit": "m/s", "stations": [["north roof", [12, 9, 15]], ["south roof", [4, 7, 5]]]}}`; typed validation supplies the declared Python tuples.

For a new extraction signature, named station records with `name: str` and `samples: list[int]` are clearer than positional pairs: the model sees each field's meaning, and the caller need not remember tuple positions. A brief instruction to preserve sample order and use one record per station would clarify that schema. Tuples remain useful when downstream code already consumes `(label, samples)` pairs; switching to records changes that contract or requires a caller-side conversion. Selecting `dspy.JSONAdapter()` instead keeps the existing typed tuple contract while asking for JSON arrays, avoiding this XML-specific traversal path. That is a public alternative, not a claim of universal provider schema support or live-model success.

Classification remains a genuine, fixture-proven positional-schema decoding defect in a plausible labeled-series workflow, not a contrived-only case. Named fields are a preferable starting design here, but do not invalidate supported tuples. Prompt changes cannot repair decoding of a valid response that the adapter itself also formats. This audit adds no live-model runs or new alternative-schema tests; historical compatibility evidence and its limits remain below.

### Central live follow-up — bounded observations, not a demonstrated fix benefit

The coordinator subsequently reported a completed six-call `gpt-6-luna` batch shared across R2, R10, R5 and their controls. For this tuple-based task, the model emitted named `<name>`/`<wind_speeds>` children instead of positional tuple `<item>` elements. Replaying the identical response failed on both [pre-fix main 0cae9e00](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/0cae9e00e1afd02202b1c61ee81693371c40afef) and [fixed 0df22438](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/0df224386787263cea8bf706651fc01dd39408d9). The simpler named `Station(name, samples)` control naturally returned the correct unit and both measurement series and passed on pre-fix main.

Thus this small live batch did **not** trigger the exact positional-schema failure this PR fixes or establish a zero-shot live benefit. The deterministic typed-contract proof remains valid, but the observed named-field response is not evidence that this tuple patch improves live task completion. These are coordinator-reported observations, not additional calls or replays by this PR owner. The completed [coordinator ledger revision 47](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/dspy-3-5-robustness-findings-and-public-api-repros-e6ba81ed-5781-492e-9572-b7564bd0788b) records all six receipts, replay logs and aggregate accounting (access may be restricted; the link follows the current revision). No fix broadening or model-reliability claim follows from this batch.

## Why positional schemas must reach all XML readers

JSON Schema uses `items` for homogeneous arrays and `prefixItems` for fixed tuple positions. The old XML code only consulted `items`, so it lost the type of each tuple position. Without the list schema, nested `item` tags become ordinary object keys; without a string schema, literal markup can be mistaken for structure.

The **+13/−7 production-line change** stays inside XMLAdapter and makes four existing paths understand `prefixItems`:

1. Value reconstruction decodes each element with its positional schema, retaining `items` for homogeneous arrays.
2. Parser traversal chooses the positional schema for an actual `item` child, so the parser knows whether that position is literal text or nested structure.
3. Delimiter recognition reads the positional schemas too, preventing literal closing-tag content from being cut at a false boundary.
4. The prompt skeleton illustrates each fixed position rather than a single untyped example item.

Only actual `item` children consume positional traversal schemas. An earlier candidate used an object's property count as the tuple index while reading repeated-field shorthand, so its second property selected the wrong tuple position. Independent review exposed that compatibility failure. The final guard preserves shorthand such as a repeated `pair` containing a two-property object followed by another `pair` containing text; a retained public streaming test also checks the following output field is still emitted.

No new public API, dependency or cross-layer parser abstraction is introduced. Top-level tuples retain their existing JSON-literal representation.

## Recorded before/after proof

These are **historical implementation-run results**, not a fresh suite run for this description edit. Baseline production was [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b). The final regression test file was copied into a disposable baseline worktree; production was left unchanged. Fixed code/tests are at [cac793ee4bdf0e87888df6a55387d6aae9eadd8a](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/cac793ee4bdf0e87888df6a55387d6aae9eadd8a). Both worktrees used the same development interpreter.

Before (summary output; long tracebacks omitted):

```console
$ /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/adapters/test_xml_adapter.py -k 'positional_tuple or repeated_tuple' -q --tb=short
8 failed, 5 passed, 86 deselected in 1.12s
```

After, including all thirteen new cases and existing adapter/Predict/streaming coverage:

```console
$ /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/adapters tests/predict/test_predict.py tests/streaming -q --tb=short
824 passed, 3 skipped, 11 warnings in 13.10s
```

| Retained tests | Baseline | Fixed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| String/list positions in either order, including empty nested list; compact/multiline XML | 6 fail | 6 pass |
| Homogeneous and empty tuple controls; compact/multiline XML | 4 pass | 4 pass |
| Independent XML, positional prompt skeleton, invalid tuple arity | 1 fail | 1 pass |
| Literal closing tag inside tuple string | 1 fail | 1 pass |
| Repeated tuple-object fields followed by a streamed answer | 1 pass | 1 pass |

The last row was a passing base behavior that the first candidate broke; the final test consumes public `streamify`, checks the final typed prediction, and concatenates actual answer chunks to `right`. It is not satisfied merely by the final Prediction object. The arity test rejects both missing and extra tuple positions. The original seven-case default/XML/Chat/JSON repro and top-level tuple/homogeneous-list controls all passed after the fix.

Independent read-only follow-up review found no blockers after **168 streaming-boundary probes** across typed shapes, literal payloads, compact/multiline layouts and chunk sizes, plus five top-level/homogeneous controls and five invalid-structure/type controls. Ruff, ty and whitespace checks passed. Those probes are bounded validation, not exhaustive XML/schema coverage.

## Complete public-API reproduction: labeled wind-measurement series

Save as `test_measurement_series_repro.py` and run `.venv/bin/python -m pytest test_measurement_series_repro.py -q -s --tb=short`. The input, typed output and public `Predict` call describe a plausible notes-to-chart workflow. `FixtureEngine` supplies hand-written XML to isolate decoding; **it does not demonstrate live-model extraction accuracy**. The test checks the two labeled series, one engine request, and an adapter-formatted round-trip. All helpers/imports are inline, with no internals patched or credentials/network calls required. XML and disabled fallback are explicit so a second JSON response cannot conceal the first parse failure.

```python
import dspy
from pydantic import BaseModel
from dspy.lm15 import Message, Response, Usage


class WindReport(BaseModel):
    unit: str
    stations: list[tuple[str, list[int]]]


class ExtractWindSeries(dspy.Signature):
    """Extract each station's name and ordered wind-speed samples from the field notes."""
    field_notes: str = dspy.InputField()
    report: WindReport = dspy.OutputField()


class FixtureEngine:
    """Return hand-written measurement XML, not live model extraction."""
    def __init__(self, wire):
        self.wire = wire
        self.calls = 0

    def complete(self, request):
        self.calls += 1
        return Response(None, request.model, Message.assistant(self.wire), "stop", Usage())


def test_labelled_measurement_series():
    notes = (
        "Wind speeds in m/s at 10:00, 10:10 and 10:20: "
        "north roof 12, 9, 15; south roof 4, 7, 5."
    )
    wire = """<report><unit>m/s</unit><stations>
<item><item>north roof</item><item><item>12</item><item>9</item><item>15</item></item></item>
<item><item>south roof</item><item><item>4</item><item>7</item><item>5</item></item></item>
</stations></report>"""
    expected = WindReport(unit="m/s", stations=[("north roof", [12, 9, 15]), ("south roof", [4, 7, 5])])
    engine = FixtureEngine(wire)
    lm = dspy.LM("custom/measurement-fixture", engine=engine, cache=False)
    adapter = dspy.XMLAdapter(use_json_adapter_fallback=False)
    with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=adapter):
        result = dspy.Predict(ExtractWindSeries)(field_notes=notes)
    assert result.report == expected
    assert engine.calls == 1
    formatted = adapter.format_assistant_message_content(ExtractWindSeries, {"report": expected})
    assert adapter.parse(ExtractWindSeries, formatted)["report"] == expected
    print(f"unit={result.report.unit}; stations={result.report.stations}; requests={engine.calls}")
```

title: Preserve tool error status in native history replay
body:
## Order lookup failures lose their error status during support-agent replay

A customer asks, “Please check my orders ORD-1040, ORD-1042, and ORD-1043.” The support agent calls the existing `lookup_order` tool for each order. One number is not found, one order is shipped, and the service is temporarily unavailable for the third:

| Call ID | Real tool invocation | Outcome | Required `is_error` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `call_order_1040` | `lookup_order(order_id="ORD-1040")` | `ValueError`: order not found; check the number | `True` |
| `call_order_1042` | `lookup_order(order_id="ORD-1042")` | `{"order_id": "ORD-1042", "status": "shipped"}` | `False` |
| `call_order_1043` | `lookup_order(order_id="ORD-1043")` | `ConnectionError`: service temporarily unavailable; retry later | `True` |

No nonexistent tool or malformed invocation is needed. These are ordinary tool execution outcomes that a support service must distinguish before responding or deciding whether to retry.

ReAct records `[True, False, True]` in History on both versions, but the baseline's next Anthropic HTTP request has no `is_error` fields: all three results are treated as successes. After the fix, the HTTP flags are `[True, False, True]`, with the same call IDs, error text, and successful order contents.

### Task realism and simpler alternatives

An ordinary useful answer is “ORD-1042 has shipped. Please check ORD-1040's number; I couldn't check ORD-1043 because the order service is temporarily unavailable.” If application policy permits, the agent could retry the transient failure; it should not treat either failure as a successful order lookup. The fixture's final answer follows this pattern but is scripted: it does not demonstrate an actual retry or improved model recovery.

A single registered `lookup_order` raising an ordinary order-not-found exception is enough to encounter this status-loss path; the three-order batch is a stronger control that checks failed results without incorrectly marking the successful result as failed. That simpler single-order variant was not separately executed. A model may also infer failure from the preserved error text and answer correctly before this fix, so this is not evidence that baseline agents necessarily give wrong answers. Returning an explicit application-level error dictionary instead of raising, or using text-mode interaction, can communicate failure but changes the tool/error protocol rather than preserving native `is_error`. Direct `LM` requests with explicit native result flags already work, as the executed controls show, at the cost of managing the tool loop and messages outside ReAct.

**Classification:** a realistic support-tool failure with a deterministic native-status propagation defect, not a contrived-only model-output case. No malformed arguments or nonexistent tools are required. The loopback proof establishes the outbound status mismatch and its correction, not live-provider acceptance or model recovery quality. No live-model evidence is available or needed to establish this invariant. This description-only audit adds no executions; the pinned results below remain the previously recorded runs.

## Why the flag is lost, and why this precise fix works

`History.format` owns translation from recorded events into native messages. When constructing each `tool_result`, it forwarded the ID, content, and name but omitted the recorded `is_error`. The native helper defaults that argument to `False`. The helper and Anthropic encoder already support error flags; replay was the missing step.

The production change is one forwarded keyword, **3 added / 1 removed lines** in `dspy/adapters/types/history.py`:

```diff
-                        tool_result(result.call_id, _tool_result_content(result.value), name=result.name)
+                        tool_result(
+                            result.call_id, _tool_result_content(result.value), name=result.name, is_error=result.is_error
+                        )
```

History already has authoritative execution status, so there is no need to infer errors from text or add a provider-specific rule. Successful results retain `False`; absent status retains the existing default. Text replay, contents, ID validation, serialization, and retry policy are unchanged.

## Fresh execution of the exact order-support reproduction

The full inline snippet below was executed unchanged on baseline [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b) and fixed revision [4407725ad5a7d324239dfc7db2c9c44b20af8d64](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/4407725ad5a7d324239dfc7db2c9c44b20af8d64). These fresh results replace the synthetic scenario as the public reproduction; older implementation evidence is retained separately below. No production or repository test files were changed.

The matrix covers sync/async ReAct and sync/async direct-LM controls. Direct controls bypass History by supplying explicit native results with the same realistic failure/success pattern; both pass even before the fix. This distinguishes a replay defect from a provider encoder defect.

Exact commands and selected recorded output, after copying the same snippet to `.amp/in/test_support_errors_repro.py` in each pinned worktree:

```console
# Working directory: /tmp/dspy-support-base
$ git rev-parse HEAD

$ PYTHONPATH="$PWD" /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -c 'import dspy; print(dspy.__file__)'
/tmp/dspy-support-base/dspy/__init__.py
$ env -u OPENAI_API_KEY -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY PYTHONPATH="$PWD" LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/test_support_errors_repro.py -q -s --tb=short
entry_point=react async=False is_error=[False, False, False]
Fentry_point=direct-lm async=False is_error=[True, False, True]
.entry_point=react async=True is_error=[False, False, False]
Fentry_point=direct-lm async=True is_error=[True, False, True]
.
E   assert [False, False, False] == [True, False, True]
2 failed, 2 passed in 2.51s

# Working directory: /tmp/dspy-support-errors
$ git rev-parse HEAD
4407725ad5a7d324239dfc7db2c9c44b20af8d64
$ PYTHONPATH="$PWD" /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -c 'import dspy; print(dspy.__file__)'
/tmp/dspy-support-errors/dspy/__init__.py
$ env -u OPENAI_API_KEY -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY PYTHONPATH="$PWD" LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/test_support_errors_repro.py -q -s --tb=short
entry_point=react async=False is_error=[True, False, True]
.entry_point=direct-lm async=False is_error=[True, False, True]
.entry_point=react async=True is_error=[True, False, True]
.entry_point=direct-lm async=True is_error=[True, False, True]

4 passed in 2.62s
```

Each case asserts the ordered call IDs and contents as well as flags. The successful middle result must remain `False`, so marking every result as failed cannot pass. ReAct cases separately check that History recorded the correct flags before examining HTTP.

## Complete runnable order-support workflow and controls

Save this exact code as `.amp/in/test_support_errors_repro.py` in a DSPy checkout with its development environment and pytest installed. Run `.venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/test_support_errors_repro.py -q -s --tb=short` from that checkout.

The real APIs exercised are public `ReAct`/`acall`, ordinary Tool invocation and exception handling, History native replay, public `LM`/`Request` controls, and `lm15`'s Anthropic HTTP encoding. The loopback server replaces the external model; the local order function replaces an external order database/service. ReAct registers every tool named in its model replies. No provider credentials or paid calls are used.

**Limit:** the server scripts the final response on both versions. Assertions about that answer are completion controls, not evidence of a model reading the flags or recovering better. The test proves preservation of structured execution status on the outbound wire; it does not test a live model, network-outage handling inside a real order client, or recovery quality.

```python
import asyncio
import json
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

import dspy
import pytest
from dspy.lm15 import Message, Request, TextPart, ToolCallPart, ToolResultPart


@pytest.fixture
def support_endpoint():
    requests = []

    class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def log_message(self, *args):
            pass

        def do_POST(self):
            body = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"])))
            requests.append(body)
            calls = [
                ("call_order_1040", "lookup_order", {"order_id": "ORD-1040"}),
                ("call_order_1042", "lookup_order", {"order_id": "ORD-1042"}),
                ("call_order_1043", "lookup_order", {"order_id": "ORD-1043"}),
            ] if len(requests) == 1 else [
                ("call_support_reply", "submit", {"answer":
                    "ORD-1042 has shipped. Please check ORD-1040's number; ORD-1043 needs a retry."}),
            ]
            payload = json.dumps({
                "id": f"msg_{len(requests)}", "type": "message", "role": "assistant", "model": body["model"],
                "content": [{"type": "tool_use", "id": call_id, "name": name, "input": arguments}
                            for call_id, name, arguments in calls],
                "stop_reason": "tool_use", "stop_sequence": None,
                "usage": {"input_tokens": 20, "output_tokens": 10},
            }).encode()
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(payload)

    server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
    worker = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
    worker.start()
    try:
        yield f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}", requests
    finally:
        server.shutdown()
        server.server_close()
        worker.join()


@pytest.mark.parametrize("entry_point", ["react", "direct-lm"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("asynchronous", [False, True])
def test_order_lookup_error_status(support_endpoint, entry_point, asynchronous):
    base, requests = support_endpoint

    def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
        """Read an order from the customer's order service."""
        if order_id == "ORD-1040":
            raise ValueError("Order ORD-1040 was not found. Check the order number.")
        if order_id == "ORD-1043":
            raise ConnectionError("Order service temporarily unavailable for ORD-1043. Please retry later.")
        assert order_id == "ORD-1042"
        return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped"}

    lm = dspy.LM("anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5", engine="lm15", api_base=base,
                 api_key="local-fixture-token", cache=False)
    question = "Please check my orders ORD-1040, ORD-1042, and ORD-1043."
    if entry_point == "react":
        agent = dspy.ReAct("question -> answer", tools=[lookup_order], max_iters=2)
        with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=dspy.ChatAdapter(use_native_function_calling=True)):
            result = asyncio.run(agent.acall(question=question)) if asynchronous else agent(question=question)
        assert result.answer == "ORD-1042 has shipped. Please check ORD-1040's number; ORD-1043 needs a retry."
        recorded = result.history.messages[0]["tool_calls"].tool_call_results.tool_call_results
        assert [result.is_error for result in recorded] == [True, False, True]
        assert len(requests) == 2
    else:
        # Control: pass explicit native results directly to LM, bypassing History replay.
        calls = [ToolCallPart(id=f"call_order_{number}", name="lookup_order", input={"order_id": f"ORD-{number}"})
                 for number in (1040, 1042, 1043)]
        results = [
            ToolResultPart(id="call_order_1040", name="lookup_order", is_error=True,
                           content=[TextPart("Order ORD-1040 was not found. Check the order number.")]),
            ToolResultPart(id="call_order_1042", name="lookup_order", is_error=False,
                           content=[TextPart('{"order_id": "ORD-1042", "status": "shipped"}')]),
            ToolResultPart(id="call_order_1043", name="lookup_order", is_error=True,
                           content=[TextPart("Order service temporarily unavailable for ORD-1043. Please retry later.")]),
        ]
        request = Request(model=lm.model, messages=(Message.user(question), Message.assistant(calls), Message.tool(results)))
        asyncio.run(lm.acall(request)) if asynchronous else lm(request)
        assert len(requests) == 1

    wire = [block for message in requests[-1]["messages"] for block in message["content"]
            if isinstance(block, dict) and block.get("type") == "tool_result"]
    assert [block["tool_use_id"] for block in wire] == ["call_order_1040", "call_order_1042", "call_order_1043"]
    assert "Order ORD-1040 was not found" in wire[0]["content"]
    assert json.loads(wire[1]["content"]) == {"order_id": "ORD-1042", "status": "shipped"}
    assert "Order service temporarily unavailable for ORD-1043" in wire[2]["content"]
    flags = [block.get("is_error", False) for block in wire]
    print(f"entry_point={entry_point} async={asynchronous} is_error={flags}")
    assert flags == [True, False, True]

```

## Historical implementation evidence — earlier synthetic probe

These are preserved **historical implementation-run results**, not results from the newly executed order-support workflow above. The baseline was [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b), including GEPA graduation. The patch was committed as [4407725ad5a7d324239dfc7db2c9c44b20af8d64](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/4407725ad5a7d324239dfc7db2c9c44b20af8d64). The former synthetic HTTP scenario and broader suites below were not rerun in this update.

The **same real-HTTP probe command** was run before and after. Both sync and async ReAct cases failed before; direct-LM controls passed. Those controls bypass History by constructing an explicit native error result, showing that the provider backend could already encode the flag.

```console
# Before: unchanged baseline production code
$ LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True .venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/release_3_5_state_stream.py -k 'tool_error_flag' -q --tb=short
E   assert [False, False, False] == [True, False, True]
FAILED .amp/in/release_3_5_state_stream.py::test_react_tool_error_flags_reach_anthropic_wire[False]
FAILED .amp/in/release_3_5_state_stream.py::test_react_tool_error_flags_reach_anthropic_wire[True]
2 failed, 2 passed, 74 deselected in 2.75s

# After: final patch
$ LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True .venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/release_3_5_state_stream.py -k tool_error_flag -q --tb=short
....                                                                     [100%]
4 passed, 74 deselected in 2.74s
```

The output is excerpted to the decisive assertion and summaries. Both runs use the real `lm15` Anthropic backend against a loopback HTTP server, not a mocked request formatter. The ReAct assertions also verify the three call IDs in order, preserved failure text, exactly two requests, and the successful final answer.

The retained repository regression uses a caller-owned LM engine to cover public ReAct/`acall` across Chat, JSON, and XML adapters. On unchanged production code:

```console
$ LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/predict/test_react.py -k native_replay_preserves_tool_error_status -q --tb=short
6 failed, 67 deselected in 0.70s
```

All six cases pass after the fix. They are included in the recorded broader run:

```console
$ env -u OPENAI_API_KEY -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/adapters tests/predict/test_react.py tests/streaming/test_react_native_tool_stream.py -q --tb=short
573 passed, 1 skipped, 10 warnings in 3.49s

$ env -u OPENAI_API_KEY -u ANTHROPIC_API_KEY PATH="/usr/bin:$PATH" LITELLM_LOCAL_MODEL_COST_MAP=True .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests -q -n 4 --tb=short
3436 passed, 740 skipped, 2 xfailed, 50 warnings in 51.59s
```

The focused skip is a live-provider test, and its warnings are existing TwoStepAdapter deprecations. The full-suite skips/xfails remain visible above; this is not a claim that every optional integration ran. [CI logs for this exact head](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/actions/runs/42677249704) provide additional coverage.


## Compatibility, review, and limits

- Mixed successes/failures distinguish this fix from marking every tool as failed. Direct-LM controls distinguish replay loss from a provider encoder defect. The committed tests additionally verify success value `22`, original IDs/order, and failure content across all three adapters.
- `uv run --locked --extra dev ty check`, production Ruff, and whitespace checks passed during implementation. Independent read-only review found the change minimal at the correct owner with no blockers; that reviewer inspected baseline logs and source but did not independently execute tests.
- Final delivery inspection recorded 25 successful checks, an expected publishing skip, and Greptile 5/5 on the head above. These are historical statuses, not a fresh CI run caused by this description edit.
- Historical investigation reproduced this in opt-in ReActV2 before promotion. The direct before/after comparison here is against the explicitly named main baseline, not a new bisect or older-release run.
- Local validation used no provider credentials or paid calls. The loopback fixture proves request construction and HTTP encoding, not live-provider acceptance, a particular model's error recovery, or recovery quality.
- This changes neither retries nor text-based error inference. It does not repair serialized call IDs; that independent defect has separate PR #10844. No Tool/schema validation or RLM history policy is changed.

title: fix(tool): accept date RootModel arguments without weakening numeric validation
body:
## A booking tool rejects the application's already-validated appointment date

An appointment application validates a form's requested date with `BookingDate.model_validate("2026-11-09")`, then calls an `available_slots(day: BookingDate)` function also exposed as a `dspy.Tool`. A Python caller reasonably reuses the validated domain object instead of serializing it to text and parsing it again. An LM/JSON caller sends the ISO string. Both should reach the same calendar lookup.

`BookingDate` is a `RootModel[date]`: it keeps date operations available in Python while its ordinary API/cache serializer emits an ISO date, not an object with a `root` key. The example performs a read-only availability lookup, not an actual booking. Calling the function directly returns the expected slots; wrapping it in Tool rejects the same valid object before the function runs:

```text
Expected slots for 2026-11-09: ["09:30", "14:00"]
Actual exception: ValueError: Arg day is invalid: datetime.date(2026, 11, 9) is not of type 'string'
```

Both synchronous calls and awaited `acall` fail for the model instance. The ISO string `"2026-11-09"` already works in both modes. This is not a claim that ordinary JSON-originated date arguments are broken.

## Task realism and simpler public approaches

For “What appointments are available on November 9, 2026?”, an ordinary LM tool call supplies `{"day":"2026-11-09"}` and receives `["09:30","14:00"]`. **That JSON argument path already passes the deterministic baseline controls.** The model is not expected to generate a Python `BookingDate` instance. The failing path is application code reusing a validated object from a form/API boundary through the same public Tool wrapper.

- For an LM-only integration, sending the ISO string is the simpler appropriate approach and the existing verified control. A new API need not introduce RootModel or a custom serializer just for this lookup. Passing an existing object's ISO value also avoids this failure, but adds serialization/parsing to the Python caller rather than preserving the typed-input contract.
- A named request model with a `day` field is another API design, but changes the scalar-root shape and caller type; it is not a drop-in repair. The current tool already has a named `day` argument, and RootModel has a legitimate role when the application already uses a scalar date domain type.
- No signature wording or adapter change is needed to produce the ordinary JSON call. Neither fixes direct Python `tool(day=requested_day)` validation, which fails without any model or adapter involved.

**Classification unchanged, scope explicit:** a typed Python-argument compatibility regression, not demonstrated failure of ordinary LM-generated JSON arguments or live provider acceptance. The shared application/tool use is plausible, but the domain wrapper is optional for an LM-only setup. Dishonest serializers and mutated numeric roots are deliberately adversarial secondary controls, not the user story or separate release findings. No alternative setup or provider call was newly executed in this audit.

Historical investigation identified this as a regression after #10828: its original four-case public probe passed on parent [25f81a83a7a4d32ed7870de7c83602148c744a10](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/25f81a83a7a4d32ed7870de7c83602148c744a10). The directly recorded before/after implementation evidence below uses the explicitly named later main baseline; this description update did not repeat that earlier parent comparison or perform a new bisect.

## Why the valid date is rejected, and why this fixes it

`Tool._validate_and_parse_args` first builds a schema-validation representation with `_json_schema_instance`, validates it against the argument's JSON Schema, then parses the original argument and calls the function. Pydantic describes a date as a JSON string with `format: date`.

The RootModel branch previously unwrapped `.root` and recursed without converting a raw Python date into JSON form. Ordinary model fields already used `_json_field_value` for that conversion, but a scalar root bypassed the field path. The result was a Python `date` checked against a JSON `string` schema.

The **+8/−4 production-line fix** propagates the root model's bytes-encoding mode through the existing container recursion and applies the existing field conversion to root leaves. It changes only the validation representation, not the original object passed to the wrapped function.

```diff
-        return _json_schema_instance(value.root)
+        return _json_schema_instance(value.root, type(value).model_config.get("ser_json_bytes", "utf8"))
```

Two compatibility decisions are necessary:

- Do not simply trust `model_dump(mode="json")` or an arbitrary custom serializer. A serializer returning `0` for `Count(4)` must not conceal a root that violates the tool's `maximum: 3` constraint.
- Preserve `numbers.Number` leaves, including Decimal and Fraction, instead of serializing them to strings or coercing them to floats. JSON Schema already validates these numeric values. Turning a constrained Decimal into a string can select the schema's string alternative and bypass a numeric maximum; an existing Pydantic instance is not automatically revalidated deeply afterward.

The change belongs in Tool argument normalization, shared by sync and async calls. It does not alter model serializers, globally enable instance revalidation, change function argument values, or modify ToolCalls/history serialization or ReAct trace mutation.

```python
import asyncio
from datetime import date

import pytest
from pydantic import RootModel, model_serializer

import dspy


class BookingDate(RootModel[date]):
    """Validated calendar date shared by the booking form and scheduling tools."""

    @model_serializer
    def serialize(self):
        # The application's API/cache representation is an ISO date, not an object.
        return self.root.isoformat()


@pytest.mark.parametrize("asynchronous", [False, True], ids=["sync", "async"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("representation", ["model", "json"], ids=["validated-date", "iso-control"])
def test_booking_availability(asynchronous, representation):
    # A form/API boundary has already validated the requested date.
    requested_day = BookingDate.model_validate("2026-11-09")
    assert requested_day.model_dump() == "2026-11-09"

    # Deterministic, read-only fixture standing in for the application's calendar.
    # Different dates have different slots so a wrong date cannot pass unnoticed.
    calendar = {

    }

    def available_slots(day: BookingDate) -> list[str]:
        """Return appointment slots without making a reservation."""
        return calendar.get(day.root, [])

    # The validated object works when the application calls the function directly.
    assert available_slots(requested_day) == ["09:30", "14:00"]
    tool = dspy.Tool(available_slots)
    # A Python caller reuses its domain object; an LM/JSON caller sends ISO text.
    argument = requested_day if representation == "model" else "2026-11-09"
    slots = asyncio.run(tool.acall(day=argument)) if asynchronous else tool(day=argument)
    assert slots == ["09:30", "14:00"]
```

title: fix(tool): preserve nested refs in ReAct submit declarations
body:
## Extracting an order's shipping contact advertises an invalid nested schema

An order-processing application uses `dspy.ReAct` to turn a shipping note into a typed `ShippingContact` containing an `Address`. This is an ordinary reason to use nested Pydantic outputs: downstream label generation needs separate street, city, region, and postal-code fields, not an unstructured answer string.

The example input is `Order SO-1042: ship to Maya Chen, 12 Harbor Road, Portland, ME 04101, US.` The expected contact is Maya Chen at that address, with the postal code preserved as the string `"04101"`. A valid native submit schema should accept that contact and reject an integer postal code that loses the leading zero.

Instead, the advertised declaration places the `Address` definition under `properties.contact.$defs` but points at the document root:

```diff
- "$ref": "#/$defs/Address"
+ "$ref": "#/properties/contact/$defs/Address"
```

Expected: validating the extracted `{"contact": ...}` against the actual native declaration succeeds. Actual on the baseline: `PointerToNowhere: '/$defs/Address' does not exist`.

**This is a JSON Schema correctness defect, not demonstrated universal provider rejection.** In the recorded caller-owned-engine test, ReAct returns the correct typed answer even before the fix; the failing assertion validates the actual advertised schema. An earlier live Azure control also accepted the malformed schema. No provider rejection rate is claimed.

## Task realism and simpler public approaches

An ordinary model response is a `submit` call with arguments `{"contact":{"name":"Maya Chen","address":{"street":"12 Harbor Road","city":"Portland","region":"ME","postal_code":"04101","country":"US"}}}`. The model need not invent schema references or emit Python objects; `$ref` is part of DSPy's request declaration, constructed before any model response. All requested facts are in the note. The deterministic engine supplies this ordinary response; it does not establish live extraction quality or provider acceptance.

- For this fully specified, one-shot extraction, **`dspy.Predict(ExtractShippingContact)` with `dspy.JSONAdapter()` is the simpler setup to consider**. ReAct is unnecessary unless the larger workflow needs tool use or iteration. This is a design recommendation, not a newly tested provider workaround; the fixture intentionally exercises the supported ReAct submit boundary.
- Flat string output fields would avoid these nested-model references, but require reconstructing the grouped contact/address API. Merely naming or renaming the nested models does not help: `ShippingContact` and `Address` are already named. Native declarations still need valid references when callers retain that typed structure.
- The recorded text-mode ReAct control already passes. Better extraction instructions cannot repair a malformed declaration, and switching adapters while still emitting the same native submit declaration is not a reference fix.

**Classification unchanged:** a deterministic native-schema correctness/portability defect with a plausible output shape, not a demonstrated failed live-LM task. The no-tool ReAct fixture is deliberately more machinery than this standalone extraction needs; that limits the task-impact claim, not the schema invariant. It is not dependent on contrived model output. This audit reuses the recorded checks; no runtime or provider tests were newly run.

## Why the references break, and why this fixes them

ReAct builds each submit argument from a standalone Pydantic schema. A local reference such as `#/$defs/Address` is valid while that argument schema is the document root. `Tool.as_function_tool()` then places the argument schema inside the complete tool parameter object's `properties`, without previously moving its references. JSON Pointer references beginning with `#/` resolve from the document root, not from the nearest object containing `$defs`.

The fix belongs at that embedding boundary, not in output parsing or a provider adapter. It copies the schema structure and prefixes local references with the argument's new location. `Tool.args` stays unchanged so per-argument validation still uses its original, standalone schema.

The production diff is **+28/−1 lines** in `dspy/adapters/types/tool.py`. The extra handling beyond the preferred 20-line target preserves demonstrated compatibility:

- Visit schema-bearing keywords, not literal data in `const`, `enum`, defaults, examples, or extensions. A literal `{"$ref": "#/literal"}` must remain literal data.
- Stop at `$id` resource boundaries, whose references already have their own root.
- Escape argument names as JSON Pointer segments and URI fragments; names containing `~`, `/`, or `%` cannot be concatenated unchanged.
- Relocate bare `#` references as well as `#/...` references. Do not expand references, so recursive schemas remain finite and definitions with the same name in separate arguments stay separate.

This does not change the reference-expansion resolver addressed independently in #10782. Expanding recursive references instead would introduce that resolver's separate recursion problem. History serialization and ReAct trace mutation are untouched.

## Historical implementation evidence (original model/list cases)

These are **historical implementation-run results**, not new test executions performed for this description update. The baseline was main [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b), including GEPA graduation. The final patch is head [93a0d0b6b17ca738fc01616ab9d929a4c343a693](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/93a0d0b6b17ca738fc01616ab9d929a4c343a693).

```console
$ .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/predict/test_react.py tests/adapters/test_tool.py -k 'nested_submit_schema or preserves_schema_scopes_and_literals or preserves_recursive_argument_scopes' -q
```

## Complete shipping-contact workflow reproduction

Save this as `test_shipping_contact_repro.py` in a DSPy checkout with development dependencies. The application signature receives the actual shipping note; the deterministic engine asserts that the note reached the request and scripts the corresponding extraction. This fixture tests DSPy's request/schema construction and output parsing, **not a live model's extraction accuracy**. `tools=[]` is sufficient for a note containing the whole address: ReAct still generates its native final-output `submit` tool.

```python
import pytest
from jsonschema import ValidationError, validate
from pydantic import BaseModel

import dspy
from dspy.lm15 import Message, Response, ToolCallPart, Usage


class Address(BaseModel):
    street: str
    city: str
    region: str
    postal_code: str
    country: str


class ShippingContact(BaseModel):
    name: str
    address: Address


class ExtractShippingContact(dspy.Signature):
    """Extract the recipient and delivery address from an order's shipping note."""
    shipping_note: str = dspy.InputField()
    contact: ShippingContact = dspy.OutputField()


@pytest.mark.parametrize("native", [False, True], ids=["text-control", "native"])
def test_extract_shipping_contact(native):
    note = "Order SO-1042: ship to Maya Chen, 12 Harbor Road, Portland, ME 04101, US."
    expected = {
        "name": "Maya Chen",
        "address": {
            "street": "12 Harbor Road",
            "city": "Portland",
            "region": "ME",
            "postal_code": "04101",
            "country": "US",
        },
    }
    outputs = {"contact": expected}

    class ShippingFixtureEngine:
        """Offline fixture: scripts this note's extraction, not a live LLM."""
        supports_function_calling = True
        supports_reasoning = True

        def complete(self, request):
            assert note in "\n".join(message.text or "" for message in request.messages)
            self.request = request
            return Response(
                id=None,
                model=request.model,
                message=Message.assistant([
                    ToolCallPart(id="submit-shipping", name="submit", input=outputs)
                ]),
                finish_reason="tool_call",
                usage=Usage(),
            )

    engine = ShippingFixtureEngine()
    if native:
        lm = dspy.LM("custom/shipping-fixture", engine=engine, cache=False)
    else:
        lm = dspy.utils.DummyLM([{
            "next_thought": "The shipping note contains the complete delivery address.",
            "tool_calls": dspy.ToolCalls.from_dict_list([
                {"name": "submit", "args": outputs}
            ]),
        }])

    with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=dspy.ChatAdapter(use_native_function_calling=native)):
        result = dspy.ReAct(ExtractShippingContact, tools=[])(shipping_note=note)

    assert result.contact == ShippingContact.model_validate(expected)
    if native:
        schema = next(t.parameters for t in engine.request.tools if t.name == "submit")
        validate(outputs, schema)
        # Postal codes are strings: losing the leading zero is not a valid extraction.
        invalid = {**expected, "address": {**expected["address"], "postal_code": 4101}}
        with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
            validate({"contact": invalid}, schema)
```
