title: Fix serialized ReAct history losing tool evidence
body:
## Problem

A customer asks, “What is the shipping status of order ORD-1042?” The support agent calls `lookup_order`, which returns the order's shipped status, UPS carrier, and tracking number `1Z999AA10123456784`. The agent replies, “Your order has shipped.” A web application then saves the conversation as JSON between requests.

The customer follows up: “Please email me the tracking details for that order.” A fresh ReAct instance receives the restored History and has a `queue_tracking_email` tool. To handle this request without another lookup, the LM needs the earlier tool result. The tracking number is absent from both user questions and both final answers; it exists in the earlier order lookup.

Before this fix, the first follow-up HTTP request contains **no earlier tool results** after either supported JSON persistence path. In-memory History works. After the fix, the order result and previous submission replay with the original IDs and contents:

```text
Expected replay IDs: ["call_order_lookup", "call_status_reply"]
Before, saved/restored History: []
After, saved/restored History:  ["call_order_lookup", "call_status_reply"]
Order result: {"order_id": "ORD-1042", "status": "shipped", "carrier": "UPS",
               "tracking_number": "1Z999AA10123456784"}
```

This is a normal continuation boundary: an application stores History between customer messages and creates a new agent for the next request. Both dict JSON persistence and `History.model_dump_json()` / `History.model_validate_json()` are exercised, including actual disk write/read.

An ordinary continuation reuses the recorded tracking fact, calls the email tool, then confirms its result. Answering “What is its tracking number?” needs the same fact without an email tool. Re-querying the order, keeping history only in memory, or storing facts separately can work around the symptom, but add service calls or application-owned persistence. This is a deterministic persistence/replay failure in a realistic task, not a claim that a live model cannot solve the task another way.

## Change

`ToolCalls.serialize_model` reused the ID-free prompt representation from `ToolCalls.format()`. The saved call lost its `id`, while its result retained `call_id`. `History.format` correctly requires matching, nonempty IDs before emitting native call/result pairs; restored calls have `id=None`, so their evidence is omitted. Weakening that check would send an invalid native conversation instead of repairing persistence.

The approved redesign at [381be2ec8af905015126b899862d7d5357556a6c](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/381be2ec8af905015126b899862d7d5357556a6c) is **+42/−5 production lines** across six adapter files, reconciled with main [340deccd528805f01078113b9476e37072f75d0d](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/340deccd528805f01078113b9476e37072f75d0d):

- Canonical aggregate `ToolCalls` storage preserves exact IDs, attached results, and tool-call continuation metadata independently of `.format()`.
- Chat/JSON/XML adapters render top-level tool-call examples without call IDs/continuation, retaining attached results. Saved `Predict` demos are recognized by exact or nullable ToolCalls field annotations.
- Nested ToolCalls used as application data retain their IDs/metadata. No recursive key-name scrubbing or generic `serialize_for_json(for_prompt=...)` / Pydantic context mode remains.
- Native response parsing and History replay preserve ToolCallPart continuation through the existing serde codec. Tool schemas still exclude this protocol metadata.

Exact IDs are the conservative storage policy; native replay requires correct call/result attachment, not necessarily the provider's original spelling. The bounded live comparison below confirms remapping for two tested non-thinking configurations, not every provider protocol.

## Proof

### Current-head credential-free, socket-blocked checks

Same revised tests, unchanged production main baseline versus the published head; baseline import path was checked in its isolated worktree. Run from each source root using the existing development virtualenv and pytest-socket:

The failures demonstrate missing persisted IDs/evidence and lost native continuation. Six text-replay controls pass on the baseline. Public ReAct tests cover sync/async × object/dict/JSON × native/text; assertions inspect the continued LM request, not merely the scripted answer. Saved-demo tests cover all three adapters, both nullable spellings, attached results, nested data, and same-shaped ordinary dictionaries.

This includes 25 scratch encoder invariants: repeated same-name calls, distinct results, consistent remapping, reversed results, nested data, and synthetic protocol metadata. Independent review found and resolved saved-demo and nullable-field omissions. Final current-main integration review: **420 passed, 1 skipped; no blockers; minimal at the correct owner**. Main's #10845 schema scoping and XML tuple changes remain intact.

### Completed live comparison — no new calls for this publication

The prior local implementation on base [07fa634dc06104b03787c728de49c668d75559e7](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/07fa634dc06104b03787c728de49c668d75559e7), with the same R7 behavioral diff, made **six total real requests**: three each to Azure OpenAI `gpt-6-luna` (reasoning off) and Anthropic `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001` (no thinking). Each model generated two `lookup_order` calls; JSON-restored History then continued once with original IDs and once with consistently remapped IDs. Tools returned distinct order facts; no real email or other external action occurred.

All four continuations returned **ORD-1042 → UPS-7Q2M-8194**, **ORD-1043 → DHL-9X4N-6208**, and **4,590 cents** combined refund. Those facts were present only in prior tool results. Receipt auditing verified each request pair differed only in corresponding call/result IDs. This exercised public Predict/Tool/History and real native HTTP providers through a recording engine, not a live full-ReAct benchmark.

Cap: six requests, 1,024 output tokens and 12,000 JSON bytes per request, zero retries, concurrency one. All six succeeded. Reported usage: **4,701 input + 429 output tokens**. Estimated cost **$0.0048273** from local pricing snapshot 1.108.3; actual billed dollars are unknown. The live budget is exhausted; the current-main reconciliation ran only credential-free/socket-blocked checks. Exact prompts, wire receipts, request IDs, served models/configuration, usage, estimates and long logs are in the [review evidence](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/history-replay-fixes-review-and-verification-771731fc-1a27-4785-940d-980db8ff4834).

## Complete runnable support workflow

Save the code below as `.amp/in/test_support_history_repro.py` in a DSPy checkout with the development environment and pytest installed. Run `.venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/test_support_history_repro.py -q -s --tb=short` from that checkout.

This drives real public `ReAct`/`acall`, Tool execution, History serialization/restoration, adapter replay, and `dspy.LM(engine="lm15")` through the real Anthropic HTTP encoder. Only the external model and order/email backends are deterministic fixtures. `local-fixture-token` is a dummy string; no provider credentials, paid calls, or real email are used.

**What the fixture does not prove:** its model replies are scripted, including the tracking-email arguments. The queued-email result therefore succeeds even on the broken baseline and is only a completion control. The decisive assertion inspects the first follow-up request **before** that scripted reply, proving whether DSPy delivered the stored tracking evidence to the model. This does not measure live model dependence, answer quality, or email delivery.

```python
import asyncio
import json
import threading
from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, ThreadingHTTPServer

import dspy
import pytest


@pytest.fixture
def support_endpoint():
    requests = []
    replies = [
        ("call_order_lookup", "lookup_order", {"order_id": "ORD-1042"}),
        ("call_status_reply", "submit", {"answer": "Your order has shipped."}),
        ("call_tracking_email", "queue_tracking_email", {
            "order_id": "ORD-1042", "tracking_number": "1Z999AA10123456784",
        }),
        ("call_email_reply", "submit", {"answer": "I've queued a tracking email for your order."}),
    ]

    class Handler(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):
        def log_message(self, *args):
            pass

        def do_POST(self):
            body = json.loads(self.rfile.read(int(self.headers["Content-Length"])))
            requests.append(body)
            call_id, name, arguments = replies[len(requests) - 1]
            payload = json.dumps({
                "id": f"msg_{len(requests)}", "type": "message", "role": "assistant", "model": body["model"],
                "content": [{"type": "tool_use", "id": call_id, "name": name, "input": arguments}],
                "stop_reason": "tool_use", "stop_sequence": None,
                "usage": {"input_tokens": 20, "output_tokens": 10},
            }).encode()
            self.send_response(200)
            self.send_header("Content-Type", "application/json")
            self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(payload)))
            self.end_headers()
            self.wfile.write(payload)

    server = ThreadingHTTPServer(("127.0.0.1", 0), Handler)
    worker = threading.Thread(target=server.serve_forever, daemon=True)
    worker.start()
    try:
        yield f"http://127.0.0.1:{server.server_port}", requests
    finally:
        server.shutdown()
        server.server_close()
        worker.join()


@pytest.mark.parametrize("storage", ["object", "dict", "json"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("asynchronous", [False, True])
def test_support_followup_retains_tracking(support_endpoint, tmp_path, storage, asynchronous):
    base, requests = support_endpoint
    queued_emails = []

    def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
        """Look up an order in the support account's order store."""
        assert order_id == "ORD-1042"
        return {"order_id": order_id, "status": "shipped", "carrier": "UPS",
                "tracking_number": "1Z999AA10123456784"}

    def queue_tracking_email(order_id: str, tracking_number: str) -> str:
        """Queue a tracking update for the authenticated customer's email address."""
        queued_emails.append((order_id, tracking_number))  # Local outbox; no email is sent.
        return "Tracking email queued."

    def support_agent():
        return dspy.ReAct("question -> answer", tools=[lookup_order, queue_tracking_email], max_iters=2)

    def ask(agent, **kwargs):
        return asyncio.run(agent.acall(**kwargs)) if asynchronous else agent(**kwargs)

    lm = dspy.LM("anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-5", engine="lm15", api_base=base,
                 api_key="local-fixture-token", cache=False)
    question = "What is the shipping status of order ORD-1042?"
    followup = "Please email me the tracking details for that order."
    with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=dspy.ChatAdapter(use_native_function_calling=True)):
        first = ask(support_agent(), question=question)
        assert first.answer == "Your order has shipped."
        history = first.history
        saved = tmp_path / "support-history.json"
        if storage == "dict":
            saved.write_text(json.dumps(history.model_dump(mode="json")))
            history = json.loads(saved.read_text())
        elif storage == "json":
            saved.write_text(history.model_dump_json())
            history = dspy.History.model_validate_json(saved.read_text())
        # A fresh agent handles the next web request using the stored conversation.
        result = ask(support_agent(), question=followup, history=history)

    assert result.answer == "I've queued a tracking email for your order."
    assert queued_emails == [("ORD-1042", "1Z999AA10123456784")]
    assert "1Z999AA10123456784" not in question + followup + first.answer + result.answer
    assert len(requests) == 4
    # Inspect the first follow-up request, BEFORE its canned email-tool reply.
    wire = [block for message in requests[2]["messages"] for block in message["content"]
            if isinstance(block, dict) and block.get("type") == "tool_result"]
    ids = [block["tool_use_id"] for block in wire]
    print(f"storage={storage} async={asynchronous} replayed_ids={ids}")
    assert ids == ["call_order_lookup", "call_status_reply"]
    assert json.loads(wire[0]["content"]) == {
        "order_id": "ORD-1042", "status": "shipped", "carrier": "UPS",
        "tracking_number": "1Z999AA10123456784",
    }
    assert json.loads(wire[1]["content"]) == {"answer": "Your order has shipped."}

```

## Limits

- **Intentional compatibility change:** nested/application ToolCalls retain IDs and continuation in prompt data. Only actual top-level call examples omit them. Attached results still include their existing `call_id`; text prompts are not entirely ID-free.
- Already-saved histories lacking IDs are not repaired. History's existing ordered-ID check still rejects out-of-order result batches, although storage and native encoders retain their attachment. No scheduling or matching-policy redesign.
- Continuation preservation is scoped to ToolCallPart. No full Message/ThinkingPart reconstruction, live signed-reasoning validation, server-held session validation, or universal provider permission to rename IDs is claimed. The live pairs are two non-thinking configurations, not a benchmark.
- The historical HTTP fixture proves replay/encoding, not model dependence or real email delivery. Current offline checks remain credential-free and socket-blocked. Live evidence comes only from the separately accounted six real calls before publication reconciliation.
- Tool/schema validation and RLM persistence policy remain outside the diff. `is_error` replay (#10847) is already in main. Unsupported opaque tool results can still trigger a pre-existing stringifying fallback; arbitrary-object or standalone ToolCall serialization is not redesigned.
- Earlier investigation located this defect in opt-in ReActV2 before promotion. Historical synthetic probes, independent reviews, and earlier CI/Greptile results remain in the [evidence record](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/history-replay-fixes-review-and-verification-771731fc-1a27-4785-940d-980db8ff4834); they are not presented as results for the new head. One earlier baseline accidentally imported the edited checkout and was discarded before the retained isolated runs.

AI assistance: Amp implemented and verified this maintainer-directed fix from a release robustness sweep. Task prompt: “Fix serialized ReAct History losing tool evidence; keep prompt rendering separate from persistence; preserve public continuation and offline fail-before/pass-after HTTP evidence.”

title: fix: preserve explicit sandbox output defaults
body:
## Sandboxed predictors lose the defaults their signatures declare

A loaded Flex shipment pipeline extracts details from order emails, then formats customer-facing updates. A warehouse email says the order is packed but does not yet contain a tracking number or support contact. The nested predictor declares useful explicit defaults: `"Awaiting carrier assignment"` and `"Reply to your purchase email"`. When its extraction reply omits unavailable fields, those defaults should appear in the update.

Before this fix, running that same pipeline in the sandbox produces `SO-1042: None. Help: None.` on LocalInterpreter or `SO-1042: jsnull. Help: jsnull.` on Deno. The expected update is `SO-1042: Awaiting carrier assignment. Help: Reply to your purchase email.` A second email that supplies a tracking number and contact works before and after; running directly on the host also works. The complete workflow below exercises this through public `Flex.load_state`, real nested predictions, all three adapters, and both interpreters. Only the model replies are deterministic fixtures.

The Deno `"jsnull"` spelling is a second problem: genuine None is converted incorrectly by its transport. This PR restores the explicit non-null default; it does not fix every nullable output. That separate defect is addressed by #10852.

### Task realism and simpler alternatives

Extracting an order ID, tracking number, and contact from shipment emails is an ordinary LM task. For “Order SO-1042 is packed. We will send a tracking number when the carrier collects it,” the application's omit-unavailable policy accepts the partial extraction `{"order_id": "SO-1042"}`; deterministic application defaults then supply the customer-facing wording shown above. The LM need not invent a carrier or a contact. This is a realistic use of a saved extraction module, but **the example deliberately scripts omission with DummyLM**. It is not evidence that a live LM followed this policy, or that omission is common.

There are simpler or more constrained ways to implement this task:

- Run the extractor directly on the host if sandboxing/saved Flex execution is unnecessary; the existing host controls already preserve defaults. For these two templated emails alone, a non-LLM parser could also suffice. Neither workaround restores compatibility for an existing sandboxed module.
- Use clearer field descriptions/examples and request every output explicitly. A schema-capable provider with strict JSONAdapter output can enforce required keys: DSPy's structured-output schema lists every output property as required. That can avoid the omission path, unlike JSON mode or prompt instructions alone. The existing adapter prompts also ask for the output fields, so the example's “omit unavailable” instruction is not a guarantee of real-provider behavior. Merely switching adapters did not repair the scripted missing-field case.
- Extract factual nullable values and apply display fallbacks on the host. This cleanly separates facts from presentation, but moves the policy out of the signature. **Explicit null is not omission:** a supplied None is preserved, not replaced by `OutputField(default=...)`; a postprocessor must choose that separate null policy deliberately rather than using broad falsy-value replacement.

Classification remains **a demonstrated sandbox signature-transport compatibility regression**, not a demonstrated live-model extraction-quality defect. The workflow is plausible; the missing-response boundary is controlled. Earlier tuple/falsy-default variants are compatibility stress cases, not claims about typical shipment extraction. The initial description audit made no live calls or additional runtime tests; the separate centrally owned live check is reported below.

### One live call did not reproduce the missing-field trigger

The coordinator reports one `gpt-6-luna` call using ChatAdapter, the Shipment fields/defaults above, and the same packed-order email. The task instruction was “Extract shipment facts from the order email without inventing details,” with **no instruction to omit fields**. The model returned every field. ChatAdapter parsed the result as:

```python
{"order_id": "SO-1042", "tracking": "None", "contact": "None"}
```

Both `"None"` values are literal strings, not Python None or JSON null; no key was missing. The coordinator replayed the identical receipt unchanged through host, LocalInterpreter, and Deno on main [0cae9e00](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/0cae9e00e1afd02202b1c61ee81693371c40afef), where the R5 fix was absent, and all three paths passed. The same unmodified receipt also passed all three paths at fixed head [c74c1879f](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/c74c1879ffb12c6f8de1b056b28d307c3b6aac9c), retaining tracking/contact as literal `"None"` strings. The coordinator verified editable host and actual isolated-worker source parity.

This is **negative evidence for a natural R5 trigger in one call**, not evidence against the fixture-proven missing-field regression, and not a live extraction-quality claim. No additional calls or tests were run by this PR owner for this addition. [Coordinator ledger](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/dspy-3-5-robustness-findings-and-public-api-repros-e6ba81ed-5781-492e-9572-b7564bd0788b) (access-restricted; published revision 47 includes receipts, hashes, all nine audit classifications, and call accounting).

## Why the metadata disappears, and why this fixes it

`sandbox_guest.signature_spec` describes a guest signature using its type string, instructions, field descriptions/constraints, JSON extras, and type bindings. It previously omitted the fields' explicit defaults. `SandboxSession._signature` then reconstructed host `InputField`/`OutputField` objects without those defaults. The normal host adapter could only apply the nullable fallback None or reject a missing non-nullable field.

The production diff is **+7/−1 lines** in those two existing serialization/reconstruction owners:

- The guest includes output fields whose `field.default is not pydantic_core.PydanticUndefined`, encoding their values with the existing Wire codec. The identity check keeps falsy defaults such as `0`, `False`, and `[]`; the codec also preserves values such as tuples rather than flattening them through plain JSON.
- The host decodes that optional defaults mapping into copied field kwargs before the existing signature reconstruction. The incoming spec is not mutated, and a spec without the new mapping still follows its previous path.
- Reconstruction serves both adapter execution and trace entries, so a traced predictor subsequently called on the host retains the same defaults. Adapters remain responsible for applying defaults; no second default-application policy is added.

This deliberately reads `field.default`, not `get_default(call_default_factory=True)`. Serializing a signature must not eagerly execute arbitrary factories or repeat their side effects while recording traces.

## Historical implementation proof

The implementation run used production baseline [afaac2646](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b), including GEPA graduation #10796. The after result used the production patch subsequently committed as [c74c1879f](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/c74c1879ffb12c6f8de1b056b28d307c3b6aac9c). For the before run, the new tests were present but the production fix was not. These are retained original implementation results, separate from the fresh shipment-workflow execution below.

The same focused command was run before and after:

```console
$ PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/flex/test_flex_class_signature.py tests/predict/test_rlm.py -k 'preserves_output_defaults or preserves_explicit_output_default' --deno -q --tb=short
# Before: baseline production + regression tests
14 failed, 370 deselected in 9.63s
# After: production fix + the same regression cases
14 passed, 370 deselected in 17.60s
```

The twelve Flex cases cover Chat/XML/JSON × Local/Deno × omitted/provided outputs. They include a nullable string default, a non-nullable string default, `0`, `False`, an empty list, and a tuple. **The provided-output cases do not mean supplied values were broken:** the first call preserves the supplied values, but the test then reuses the traced predictor on the host with an omitted-field response. That second call fails before the fix. The remaining two cases exercise a predictor authored inside an RLM REPL.

The original, independently written public release probes were also rerun unchanged:

```console
$ PATH="$PWD/.venv/bin:$PATH" .venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/release_3_5_followup.py -k output_default -q --tb=short
# Before: afaac2646
9 failed, 3 passed, 60 deselected in 19.33s
# After: R5 production fix
12 passed, 60 deselected in 5.84s
```

| Original public probe | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Direct host, Chat/XML/JSON | 3 pass | 3 pass |
| Loaded Flex, nullable explicit default, Chat/XML/JSON × Local/Deno | 6 fail | 6 pass |
| Loaded Flex, non-nullable explicit default, Local/Chat | 1 fail | 1 pass |
| RLM nested predictor, Local/Deno | 2 fail | 2 pass |

## Complete public workflow: shipment email to customer update

Save this exact example as `test_shipment_updates.py`. Use a file because `inspect.getsource` reads the module's source. The loaded module loops over two actual-shaped emails, invokes its own extraction predictor, and uses the result in a customer update. DummyLM supplies deterministic extraction replies; this demonstrates what happens when unavailable fields are omitted, not how often a live provider omits them. The second order supplies both fields and guards against replacing real tracking/contact details with defaults.

```python
import inspect
import textwrap

import dspy
import pytest
from dspy.utils import DummyLM


class ShipmentDesk(dspy.Module):
    def forward(self, emails):
        class Shipment(dspy.Signature):
            """Extract shipment details from an order email. Omit unavailable details."""

            email: str = dspy.InputField()
            order_id: str = dspy.OutputField()
            tracking: str | None = dspy.OutputField(default="Awaiting carrier assignment")
            contact: str | None = dspy.OutputField(default="Reply to your purchase email")

        extract = dspy.Predict(Shipment)
        updates = []
        for email in emails:
            shipment = extract(email=email)
            updates.append(f"{shipment.order_id}: {shipment.tracking}. Help: {shipment.contact}.")
        return dspy.Prediction(updates=updates)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("factory", [None, dspy.LocalInterpreter, dspy.PythonInterpreter],
                         ids=["host-control", "local", "deno"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("adapter", [dspy.ChatAdapter(use_json_adapter_fallback=False),
                                    dspy.XMLAdapter(use_json_adapter_fallback=False), dspy.JSONAdapter()],
                         ids=["chat", "xml", "json"])
def test_customer_shipment_updates(factory, adapter):
    emails = [
        "Order SO-1042 is packed. We will send a tracking number when the carrier collects it.",
        "Order SO-1043 shipped. Track with TRK-8021. Questions: dispatch@example.com.",
    ]
    # Deterministic extraction replies, not live model output. The first omits unavailable fields.
    lm = DummyLM([
        {"order_id": "SO-1042"},
        {"order_id": "SO-1043", "tracking": "TRK-8021", "contact": "dispatch@example.com"},
    ])
    if factory is None:
        program = ShipmentDesk()
    else:
        program = dspy.Flex("emails: list[str] -> updates: list[str]", interpreter_factory=factory)
        program.load_state({"module_src": textwrap.dedent(inspect.getsource(ShipmentDesk))})
    with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=adapter):
        actual = program(emails=emails).updates
    print(f"{factory.__name__ if factory else 'host'} / {type(adapter).__name__}: {actual!r}")
    assert actual == [
        "SO-1042: Awaiting carrier assignment. Help: Reply to your purchase email.",
        "SO-1043: TRK-8021. Help: dispatch@example.com.",
    ]
```

title: fix: honor reasoning dictionaries in ChainOfThought
body:
## Problem: CoT ignores dictionary reasoning controls or loses its fallback plan

Default `ChainOfThought` exposes `dspy.Reasoning` to the caller. The adapter must choose between native reasoning and an explicit `plan` field before formatting the request. Dictionary controls were not included in that choice:

- On a reasoning-capable LM, `dspy.LM(..., reasoning={"effort": "high"})` sent **low**, not high. LM-level disabling dictionaries could also be overwritten by low.
- Disabling dictionaries supplied at predictor/call scope could correctly disable native reasoning in the request builder, while the adapter had already removed the explicit plan. Neither reasoning path then remained available.
- A non-native LM still needs the explicit plan. An empty dictionary must retain the request builder's normal default, not acquire an adapter-injected low effort.

The decisive expected results are the caller's effective request effort and a surviving reasoning path: explicit plan when native reasoning is disabled or unavailable, native summary when enabled and supplied by the engine. The offline engine below deliberately supplies a native summary even for disabled controls; that distinguishes correct fallback selection from accidentally accepting an irrelevant native part. It does not claim providers normally return such parts when disabled.

This is a default-CoT release regression: the same Responses HTTP probe preserved requested none/high on 3.4.1 but sent low on the main baseline. This does not classify all earlier opt-in `Reasoning` behavior as newly introduced.

## Change: use the request builder's existing dictionary precedence

`Reasoning.adapt_to_native_lm_feature` considered scalar `reasoning_effort` and provider `thinking`, but not `reasoning`. With neither recognized control present, it injected `reasoning_effort="low"` and removed the reasoning field. The later request merge could overwrite an LM-level dictionary with that injected alias, or honor a call-level disabling dictionary after the adapter had already removed the plan.

The fix adds nine production lines. It reads the effective dictionary through the existing `generation_options(lm, lm_kwargs)` alias merge, so adapter selection and request construction use the same LM-versus-call precedence:

```python
reasoning = generation_options(lm, lm_kwargs).get("reasoning")
if isinstance(reasoning, dict):
    if reasoning.get("enabled") is False or reasoning.get("effort") in ("none", "off") or not lm.supports_reasoning:
        return signature
    return signature.delete(field_name)
```

Disabled/native-unavailable cases retain the field for existing fallback renaming to `plan`. Enabled dictionaries use native reasoning without injecting a competing scalar default. Both accepted disabled spellings, `none` and canonical `off`, are covered. Scalar controls and request-builder validation of contradictory provider controls remain unchanged. #10615 addresses scalar `"none"` and ReAct forced submit, not these dictionary cases.

## Proof: recorded before/after results

These are historical implementation-run results, not new executions performed while expanding this description:

- Baseline production: [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b), main including GEPA graduation #10796, with the final regression tests copied in and no production fix.
- Fixed production/tests: [06e2e318c32a239e3f2dd889bbfc0c41984e3071](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/06e2e318c32a239e3f2dd889bbfc0c41984e3071), this PR's head.

The commands below are normalized reproduction commands for the recorded test selections, not verbatim historical shell transcripts. Output blocks quote the recorded result summaries separately.

Before, on the baseline with the same final tests:

```bash
.venv/bin/pytest tests/adapters/test_reasoning.py -k 'dictionary or alias_override' -q
```

Recorded output:

```text
13 failed, 21 passed, 6 deselected in 0.49s
```

After, on the fixed revision, the recorded broader run includes the focused cases plus existing scalar/provider controls. Normalized reproduction command:

```bash
.venv/bin/pytest tests/adapters tests/predict/test_chain_of_thought.py tests/clients/test_lm_call_contract.py -q
```

Recorded output:

```text
652 passed, 10 warnings in 3.59s
```

The **34 focused cases are a passing subset of that 652-test run**, not a separately recorded historical after invocation. The Fixed column below reports those included cases. The genuinely fresh standalone 34-case execution is reported separately below.

| Control group | Cases | Baseline | Fixed | Observable contract |
| --- | ---: | --- | --- | --- |
| Native-capable engine × LM/predictor/call scope × five dictionaries | 15 | 11 fail, 4 pass | 15 pass | Requested effort/summary and native-versus-explicit reasoning |
| Non-native engine × same scopes/dictionaries | 15 | 15 pass | 15 pass | Explicit plan survives even when native reasoning is unavailable |
| LM dictionary → call scalar and LM scalar → call dictionary, enabling/disabling | 4 | 2 fail, 2 pass | 4 pass | Call overrides win across aliases |
| Existing scalar/provider-thinking cases in broader suite | Included above | Compatibility controls | Pass | Includes sync/async Anthropic disabled-thinking and contradiction validation |

The five dictionaries are `{"enabled": False}`, `{"effort": "none"}`, `{"effort": "off"}`, `{"effort": "high", "summary": "detailed"}`, and `{}`. The expected canonical efforts are off/off/off/high/medium. The two failing alias cases before the fix were scalar-default → disabling dictionary and disabled-scalar-default → high dictionary.

Additional recorded evidence: the original public probe changed from **7 failed / 5 passed to 12 passed**. A loopback Responses HTTP check requested none/high; both were sent as low before, and both were sent unchanged after, with cmpnd tracing enabled on the after run. Its fixture was corrected to supply a plan when the prompt requests one; the **same corrected fixture** was run before and after. No live provider was used.

## Complete offline reproduction: route customer-support tickets

A support application routes a ticket about duplicate charges after an upgrade to the billing queue. It may request high effort for multi-issue tickets, or disable native reasoning on a fast, lower-cost routine-routing path while still retaining an explicit rationale for audit. The application can set that policy on the LM, on its routing predictor, or per call. The bug either changes the requested effort or loses the fallback rationale; simply receiving the right queue does not show the controls worked.

Save the following as `test_cot_dictionary_repro.py` in a DSPy checkout with development dependencies installed. This revised scenario preserves the 34-case control matrix. The **caller-owned deterministic engine** scripts a billing classification and two distinguishable explanations; it is not a live classifier and does not establish cost, latency, or classification accuracy. All imports and engine behavior are inline; no credentials, network access, or internal monkeypatches are needed. Historical results above refer to the original committed tests, not this revised scenario.

```python
import pytest
import dspy
from dspy.lm15 import Message, Response, TextPart, ThinkingPart, Usage


TICKET = (
    "After upgrading our team to the annual plan, my card shows two settled charges "
    "for the same invoice. Please refund the duplicate; our account still works."
)
EXPLICIT = "Duplicate settled charges require billing review, not an account-access reset."
NATIVE = "The reported problem is a duplicate payment; route it to billing for a refund review."


class RouteTicket(dspy.Signature):
    """Route a customer ticket to billing or account_access based on the action requested."""
    ticket: str = dspy.InputField()
    queue: str = dspy.OutputField()


class Engine:
    def __init__(self, native=True):
        self.supports_reasoning = native
        self.requests = []

    def complete(self, request):
        self.requests.append(request)
        plan = f"<plan>{EXPLICIT}</plan>" if "<plan>" in request.system else ""
        return Response(
            None, request.model,
            Message.assistant([
                ThinkingPart(NATIVE), TextPart(plan + "<queue>billing</queue>")
            ]),
            "stop", Usage(),
        )


@pytest.mark.parametrize("native", [False, True])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("location", ["lm", "predictor", "call"])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("reasoning,effort", [
    ({"enabled": False}, "off"),
    ({"effort": "none"}, "off"),
    ({"effort": "off"}, "off"),
    ({"effort": "high", "summary": "detailed"}, "high"),
    ({}, "medium"),
])
def test_dictionary(native, location, reasoning, effort):
    engine = Engine(native)
    options = {"reasoning": reasoning}
    lm = dspy.LM(
        "custom/support-router", engine=engine, cache=False,
        **(options if location == "lm" else {}),
    )
    cot = dspy.ChainOfThought(
        RouteTicket, **(options if location == "predictor" else {})
    )
    with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=dspy.XMLAdapter(use_json_adapter_fallback=False)):
        result = cot(ticket=TICKET, config=options if location == "call" else {})
    assert result.queue == "billing"
    assert result.reasoning == (NATIVE if native and effort != "off" else EXPLICIT)
    assert len(engine.requests) == 1
    assert engine.requests[0].config.reasoning.effort == effort
    if "summary" in reasoning:
        assert engine.requests[0].config.reasoning.summary == "detailed"


@pytest.mark.parametrize("defaults,override,effort", [
    ({"reasoning": {"effort": "high"}}, {"reasoning_effort": "none"}, "off"),
    ({"reasoning_effort": "high"}, {"reasoning": {"enabled": False}}, "off"),
    ({"reasoning": {"enabled": False}}, {"reasoning_effort": "high"}, "high"),
    ({"reasoning_effort": "none"}, {"reasoning": {"effort": "high"}}, "high"),
])
def test_alias_override(defaults, override, effort):
    engine = Engine()
    lm = dspy.LM("custom/support-router", engine=engine, cache=False, **defaults)
    with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=dspy.XMLAdapter(use_json_adapter_fallback=False)):
        result = dspy.ChainOfThought(RouteTicket)(ticket=TICKET, config=override)
    assert result.queue == "billing"
    assert result.reasoning == (EXPLICIT if effort == "off" else NATIVE)
    assert engine.requests[0].config.reasoning.effort == effort
```

Normalized reproduction command for the standalone file on either named revision, keeping the file identical (the fresh validation used isolated exports and an explicit import path, as described below):

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest test_cot_dictionary_repro.py -q --tb=short
```

**Earlier description validation (superseded example):** the prior arithmetic snippet produced `13 failed, 21 passed in 0.64s` on the baseline and `34 passed in 0.63s` on the fixed head. Those results belong to that earlier snippet, not the support-routing example now embedded here. Fresh results for the revised exact snippet are reported below.

### Fresh execution of the exact support-routing snippet

The inline Python block was extracted unchanged and executed with `-q --tb=short` against isolated exports of baseline [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b) and fixed head [06e2e318c32a239e3f2dd889bbfc0c41984e3071](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/06e2e318c32a239e3f2dd889bbfc0c41984e3071). The imported `dspy` path was verified before each run, with the same dependency environment. These are actual standalone scenario runs, not subset counts inferred from the historical broader suite.

Baseline result:

```text
13 failed, 21 passed in 0.62s
```

Fixed-head result:

```text
34 passed in 0.51s
```

The failure pattern matches the historical control matrix: native-capable LM dictionaries and two alias-override cases fail; all 15 non-native controls pass. The classification remains `billing`, but the baseline either chooses the wrong reasoning representation or sends the wrong effort. In particular, the high-effort LM case sends low instead of high. The disabled-path assertions distinguish the explicit audit rationale from the deliberately supplied native summary; that native part is a deterministic boundary-control fixture, not a claim about provider behavior.

The [committed tests](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/blob/06e2e318c32a239e3f2dd889bbfc0c41984e3071/tests/adapters/test_reasoning.py#L6-L55) remain the source for the historical matrix. The inline reproduction is complete without following that link.

## Limits and review

- No live-provider acceptance test, model-quality benchmark, provider routing change, or forced-submit policy change. Native reasoning can still be empty when a provider supplies no summary; this fix does not manufacture one.
- Local suite counts are focused coverage, not a full-repository local run. Pre-commit and ty passed. The repository's configured Ruff fix check passed; a full Ruff diagnostic also reported two unchanged warnings in the existing test file, left outside this fix.
- Independent review caught the canonical `"off"` spelling; it was added and covered, including disabled provider thinking. Follow-up review found the blocker resolved. Review was read-only; runtime evidence came from the implementation runs.
- Historical exact-head GitHub inspection found passing checks (only `publish-current` intentionally skipped) and Greptile 5/5 for [06e2e318c32a239e3f2dd889bbfc0c41984e3071](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/06e2e318c32a239e3f2dd889bbfc0c41984e3071). This description update changes no code and makes no new CI claim.

title: Fix bootstrap demo selection for multi-turn agents with callable tools
body:
## BootstrapFewShot crashes after a successful two-turn ReAct run

A support team uses a ReAct agent to look up order status, then compiles it from labeled customer-support examples with `BootstrapFewShot`. A normal request succeeds, but compiling that same two-turn workflow crashes after the teacher has already answered correctly.

The example below asks, “Has order A1042 shipped, and when should it arrive?” A module-level `lookup_order(order_id)` reads a structured order record: shipped, UPS, expected delivery `2026-11-12`. The agent submits “Order A1042 has shipped via UPS and is expected on November 12, 2026.” The metric accepts that answer. Expected: compilation returns one demonstration. Actual on the baseline:

```text
AttributeError: Can't pickle local object 'ReAct._make_submit_tool.<locals>.submit'
```

The user tool is deliberately module-level. The unpicklable closure is ReAct's internally created submit tool, so moving the user's function out of a notebook or local scope does not solve this case.

## Why selection crashes, and why this fixes it

`Predict` records each call's inputs and outputs. ReAct invokes the same predictor twice, and its inputs include the tool list. `BootstrapFewShot._bootstrap_one_example` converts the accepted trace entries to candidate demos. When a predictor has more than one candidate for that example, the optimizer seeds a local RNG with `Hasher.hash(tuple(demos))`. `Hasher` uses standard `pickle.dumps`, which cannot serialize the local submit function reachable through the tool list.

Demo selection does not need to serialize those inputs. This change seeds the RNG with the predictor name and its accepted-demo position instead, keeping the existing selection expression:

```diff
 if len(demos) > 1:
-    from dspy.utils.hasher import Hasher
-
-    rng = random.Random(Hasher.hash(tuple(demos)))
+    # Seed by position, not demo contents: inputs may contain unpicklable tools.
+    rng = random.Random(f"{name}:{len(self.name2traces[name])}")
     demos = [rng.choice(demos[:-1]) if rng.random() < 0.5 else demos[-1]]
```

The production diff is **2 additions, 3 deletions** in bootstrap selection. Half the probability still goes to the last trace; the other half is distributed among earlier traces. Single-trace behavior and demo representations are unchanged. No changes to `Hasher`, tool serialization, or ReAct's submit schema are needed.

## Historical implementation proof

This section preserves historical execution results from the implementation session; these suite runs were not repeated during the description update. The fresh order-status reproduction is recorded separately below. The production baseline was main [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b), including GEPA graduation. The patch and final tests were committed as [167f6fde465b7307a9662262eaa1f3837350cc50](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/167f6fde465b7307a9662262eaa1f3837350cc50).

**Before:** add the new public ReAct regression and repeated ordinary-Predict control to the baseline, with production code unchanged:

```console
$ .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/teleprompt/test_bootstrap.py -k 'multiturn_react or repeated_predictor' -q --tb=short
E   AttributeError: Can't pickle local object 'ReAct._make_submit_tool.<locals>.submit'
FAILED tests/teleprompt/test_bootstrap.py::test_bootstrap_multiturn_react - A...
1 failed, 1 passed, 16 deselected in 0.82s
```

The ordinary repeated-Predict control passed before the fix. The ReAct failure reached the pickle call before any compiled-demo assertions. This historical baseline run used the initial test draft; the final committed test also converts `Reasoning` to `str` for its thought assertion, after an intermediate candidate run exposed that test-only assertion error. The fresh workflow below is a separate, unchanged-before/after reproduction.

**After:** with the final patch and tests, run bootstrap, bootstrap-trace, ReAct, and ReActV2 together:

```console
$ .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/teleprompt/test_bootstrap.py tests/teleprompt/test_bootstrap_trace.py tests/predict/test_react.py tests/predict/test_react_v2.py -q --tb=short
119 passed, 1 skipped, 21 warnings in 1.57s
```

The skip was an optional image test; the warnings were ReActV2 deprecations. This is focused local coverage, not a full-repository local test claim. The original independent two-turn public reproduction also passed after the patch.

## Fresh order-status workflow: baseline fails, fixed head passes

The exact snippet below was newly executed, unchanged, against separately installed packages built from the pinned baseline and fixed head above. Execution started in `/tmp/dspy-realistic-repros`, outside the working checkout. The environments shared dependency versions, not DSPy source. SHA-256 checks for `predict/react.py`, `predict/rlm.py`, and `teleprompt/bootstrap.py` matched each archived revision in both the host and an isolated LocalInterpreter worker. No branch checkout or production edit was needed.

Decisive output excerpts (progress bars and traceback frames omitted):

```console
$ base-env/bin/python -I -m pytest test_order_status_repro.py -q -s --tb=short
Direct customer answer: Order A1042 has shipped via UPS and is expected on November 12, 2026.
E   AttributeError: Can't pickle local object 'ReAct._make_submit_tool.<locals>.submit'
1 failed in 0.41s

$ r8-env/bin/python -I -m pytest test_order_status_repro.py -q -s --tb=short
Direct customer answer: Order A1042 has shipped via UPS and is expected on November 12, 2026.
Compiled order-status demonstrations: 1
1 passed in 0.46s
```

`base-env` contains `afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b`; `r8-env` contains `167f6fde465b7307a9662262eaa1f3837350cc50`, the original PR head. This PR is now merged, but the comparison deliberately tests those exact revisions rather than attributing later main changes to this fix.

## Complete runnable order-status reproduction

Save as `test_order_status_repro.py`. With the selected DSPy revision and pytest installed in a virtual environment, run `python -I -m pytest test_order_status_repro.py -q -s --tb=short` from its directory. The in-memory order table stands in for an order-management API; the real module-level tool is executed and its structured observation checked. `DummyLM` scripts the two decisions and customer-facing wording, including the expected answer. This proves the normal public workflow can reach the crash, not that a live model will choose those calls or produce that wording.

```python
import dspy
from dspy.utils import DummyLM


ORDERS = {
    "A1042": {"status": "shipped", "carrier": "UPS", "delivery_date": "2026-11-12"},
}


def lookup_order(order_id: str) -> dict:
    """Look up fulfillment status and expected delivery for a customer's order."""
    return ORDERS[order_id]


def test_order_status_agent_can_be_bootstrapped():
    example = dspy.Example(
        question="Has order A1042 shipped, and when should it arrive?",
        answer="Order A1042 has shipped via UPS and is expected on November 12, 2026.",
    ).with_inputs("question")
    replies = [
        {
            "next_thought": "Check the order record before giving a delivery date.",
            "tool_calls": dspy.ToolCalls.from_dict_list([
                {"name": "lookup_order", "args": {"order_id": "A1042"}},
            ]),
        },
        {
            "next_thought": "The lookup says UPS has shipped the order with a November 12 delivery date.",
            "tool_calls": dspy.ToolCalls.from_dict_list([
                {"name": "submit", "args": {"answer": example.answer}},
            ]),
        },
    ]
    agent = dspy.ReAct("question -> answer", tools=[lookup_order], max_iters=2)
    adapter = dspy.ChatAdapter(use_native_function_calling=False)

    # A normal customer request works even on the affected revision.
    with dspy.context(lm=DummyLM(replies), adapter=adapter):
        result = agent(question=example.question)
    assert result.answer == example.answer
    observation = result.history.messages[0]["tool_calls"].tool_call_results.tool_call_results[0].value
    assert observation == ORDERS["A1042"]
    print("Direct customer answer:", result.answer)

    # Compile that same workflow from a labeled support example.
    with dspy.context(lm=DummyLM(replies), adapter=adapter):
        compiled = dspy.BootstrapFewShot(
            metric=lambda expected, actual, trace: actual.answer == expected.answer,
            max_bootstrapped_demos=1,
            max_labeled_demos=0,
        ).compile(agent, trainset=[example])
    assert len(compiled.react.demos) == 1
    print("Compiled order-status demonstrations:", len(compiled.react.demos))
```

The direct-call control reaches the tool and returns the expected customer answer on both revisions. Only subsequent compilation differs. The function is module-level, so the failure cannot be explained by a locally defined user tool. This revised demonstration lives in the PR description, not in a source/test-suite change.

## Controls, review, and limits

- The retained ordinary-Predict control calls one predictor three times per training example, with asymmetric `first`, `middle`, and `last` answers over 12 examples. Two compilations must preserve example order, produce the same selections, and reach all three positions. It passed on both baseline and patch.
- An independent read-only review reproduced the base closure error by loading base production code in memory. Its bootstrap/ReAct check passed **84 tests, with one optional skip**; it found no correctness blocker and judged bootstrap selection the correct owner.
- `ruff check dspy/teleprompt/bootstrap.py tests/teleprompt/test_bootstrap.py`, `uv run --locked --extra dev ty check`, and `git diff --check` passed. The implementation session also recorded green CI and Greptile **5/5 explicitly tied to the head above**; this description update does not present that historical check as a fresh CI run.
- **Exact historical demo selections change.** Recompilation stays deterministic for the same predictor names, accepted positions, and trace counts, but changing demo contents no longer changes the draw. Position-based draws correlate across structurally identical programs. For predictor name `react`, accepted positions 0–3 choose earlier traces; there is no balanced-small-sample guarantee.
- The new tests verify repeatability and reachability, not the exact 50/50 probability weight. A review mutation to uniform selection still passed them; the weighting expression itself is unchanged by this PR.
- This fixes the crash, not mutable-history target leakage, which is handled separately in #10848. No paid calls, remote training, model-quality measurements, or optimizer-convergence claims were made.

title: fix(xml): parse nested numeric and boolean literals
body:
## Nested XML Literals are rejected even when their values are allowed

Consider a support team coding a batch of survey responses for an analytics export. Each row contains the response ID, a sentiment code from `Literal[-1, 0, 1]`, and a follow-up choice from `Literal[True, False]`. A typed survey schema can represent closed options this way; an ordinary `bool` field is not the failing case. Returning `list[SurveyClassification]` from `Predict` is an ordinary batch-classification workflow.

For “My replacement arrived broken. Please contact me” and “The replacement works perfectly. No follow-up needed,” the fixture below supplies valid XML classifications with codes `[-1, 1]` and choices `[True, False]`. Before this fix, XML leaves these as strings (`'-1'`, `'1'`, `'true'`, `'false'`), and `Predict` raises `AdapterParseError` with four Literal mismatches instead of returning the typed rows. Ordinary top-level Literal parsing uses a different conversion path and already works.

The failure is visible through `Predict` when XML's JSON fallback is disabled. Fallback can otherwise hide the XML failure behind another generation; that is not successful decoding of the first response. Historical release investigation also reproduced the opt-in XML limitation before XML became the default. The before/after proof below establishes the repair against a named main revision, not a fresh bisect of the default change.

## Why the conversion belongs here

`XMLAdapter._elements_to_value` previously returned literal leaves as strings. For reconstructed dictionaries/lists, `parse` sends the whole container directly to Pydantic's `validate_python`; it does not call the scalar `parse_value` helper on each leaf. Pydantic can coerce ordinary integers there, but does not turn an arbitrary string into an integer/bool Literal member.

The change reuses `parse_value` for leaves whose schema has `enum` or `const`, before validating the enclosing container. It reconstructs a `Literal` annotation from those allowed values, so conversion uses the existing scalar Literal rules rather than a second numeric/bool parser. Production diff: **+9/−1 lines in XMLAdapter**, no dependency or public API changes.

Two guards preserve existing behavior:

- Schema enums also represent Python `Enum`. If preliminary Literal conversion fails, raw text remains available for original annotation validation, including supported Enum member names. Invalid Literal values still fail final validation.
- A selected branch of a multi-branch scalar union is not enough information to choose its result type. Coercion is disabled there; nullable Literals with only one non-null branch still convert.

For example, `list[Literal[1] | str]` with text `1` must retain the existing string result `['1']`, not become `[1]`. Greptile caught that regression in the first revision; the final revision restores it and also protects float results in `Literal[1] | float`.

## Recorded before/after proof

These are **historical implementation-run results**, not newly rerun suite results from this description edit. Baseline production was [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b); the final regression tests were copied into a disposable baseline worktree without changing its production code. The fixed code/tests are at [6d3fe15965ab43929e6e54ed311fb950336c08ca](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/6d3fe15965ab43929e6e54ed311fb950336c08ca).

Before, from the baseline worktree using the shared development interpreter (selected output; long tracebacks omitted):

```console
$ /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/adapters/test_xml_adapter.py -k 'nested_literals or literal_unions' -q --tb=short
E     Input should be -1 or 2 [type=literal_error, input_value='-1', input_type=str]
5 failed, 5 passed, 86 deselected in 0.89s
```

After, from the fixed checkout; this broader command includes all ten new cases:

```console
$ .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/adapters tests/predict/test_predict.py tests/streaming -q --tb=short
821 passed, 3 skipped, 11 warnings in 12.41s
```

| Retained public Predict cases | Baseline | Fixed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Negative/positive integer Literals, true/false bool Literals, nullable integer Literal | 5 fail | 5 pass |
| String Literal/mixed string-numeric Literal precedence | 2 pass | 2 pass |
| Multi-branch unions retain string/string/float result types | 3 pass | 3 pass |

The tests check actual Python types as well as values, one recorded request with fallback disabled, adapter-produced round-trips, and rejection of invalid Literal members. Existing Enum-name tests run in the broader suite. A separate original repro subset, including Chat/JSON controls, recorded **4 passed**. Ruff, `uv run --locked --extra dev ty check`, and whitespace checks passed. Independent read-only follow-up review and simplicity audit found no blockers and probed additional nullable, reversed-order, bool/int and float union controls.

## Complete public-API reproduction: survey classification

Save this as `test_survey_repro.py` in the checkout and run `.venv/bin/python -m pytest test_survey_repro.py -q -s --tb=short`. The signature and input are a plausible user workflow; `FixtureEngine` supplies a hand-written response only to make the adapter failure repeatable. This is **not evidence that a live model correctly classified these responses**. All imports/helpers are inline, no internals are patched, and no credentials or network calls are needed. XML is explicit and fallback disabled so an extra JSON generation cannot hide a parsing failure. Both the independently written response and an adapter-formatted round-trip are checked.

```python
from typing import Literal

import dspy
from pydantic import BaseModel
from dspy.lm15 import Message, Response, Usage


class SurveyClassification(BaseModel):
    response_id: str
    sentiment: Literal[-1, 0, 1]
    follow_up: Literal[True, False]


class ClassifySurvey(dspy.Signature):
    """Code each survey response: negative=-1, neutral=0, positive=1.
    Set follow_up from the respondent's explicit request for contact.
    """
    responses: str = dspy.InputField()
    classifications: list[SurveyClassification] = dspy.OutputField()


class FixtureEngine:
    """Return a hand-written XML fixture, not a live model classification."""
    def __init__(self, wire):
        self.wire = wire
        self.calls = 0

    def complete(self, request):
        self.calls += 1
        return Response(None, request.model, Message.assistant(self.wire), "stop", Usage())


def test_survey_classification():
    responses = (
        "R-104: My replacement arrived broken. Please contact me to arrange a return.\n"
        "R-105: The replacement works perfectly. No follow-up needed."
    )
    wire = """<classifications>
<item><response_id>R-104</response_id><sentiment>-1</sentiment><follow_up>true</follow_up></item>
<item><response_id>R-105</response_id><sentiment>1</sentiment><follow_up>false</follow_up></item>
</classifications>"""
    engine = FixtureEngine(wire)
    lm = dspy.LM("custom/survey-fixture", engine=engine, cache=False)
    adapter = dspy.XMLAdapter(use_json_adapter_fallback=False)
    with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=adapter):
        rows = dspy.Predict(ClassifySurvey)(responses=responses).classifications
    assert rows == [
        SurveyClassification(response_id="R-104", sentiment=-1, follow_up=True),
        SurveyClassification(response_id="R-105", sentiment=1, follow_up=False),
    ]
    assert all(type(row.sentiment) is int and type(row.follow_up) is bool for row in rows)
    assert engine.calls == 1
    formatted = adapter.format_assistant_message_content(ClassifySurvey, {"classifications": rows})
    assert adapter.parse(ClassifySurvey, formatted)["classifications"] == rows
    print(f"sentiment={[row.sentiment for row in rows]}; follow_up={[row.follow_up for row in rows]}; requests={engine.calls}")
```

### Newly executed scenario proof

The exact block above was run unchanged on baseline [afaac264](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b) and fixed head [6d3fe159](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/6d3fe15965ab43929e6e54ed311fb950336c08ca), using the same installed dependencies and selecting each checkout with `PYTHONPATH`. This is a new scenario run, separate from the historical ten-case matrix. The baseline was a detached worktree; no production code or maintained tests changed. Selected decisive output follows; long tracebacks are omitted.

Before, from the baseline worktree:

```console
$ PYTHONPATH="$PWD" /home/user/workspace/repo/.venv/bin/python -m pytest /home/user/workspace/repo/.amp/in/test_survey_repro.py -q -s --tb=short
E   dspy.utils.exceptions.AdapterParseError: Failed to parse field classifications: 4 validation errors for list[SurveyClassification]
E     Input should be -1, 0 or 1 [type=literal_error, input_value='-1', input_type=str]
E     Input should be True or False [type=literal_error, input_value='true', input_type=str]
1 failed in 0.67s
```

After, from the fixed checkout:

```console
$ PYTHONPATH="$PWD" .venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/test_survey_repro.py -q -s --tb=short
sentiment=[-1, 1]; follow_up=[True, False]; requests=1
1 passed in 0.53s
```

For provenance, the **earlier description's superseded synthetic snippet** had also been executed on the same fixed head. Its historical output below is retained; it is not the survey scenario above:

```console
$ PYTHONPATH="$PWD" .venv/bin/python -m pytest .amp/in/test_pr_10840_repro.py -q --tb=short
4 passed in 0.51s
```

## Compatibility and limits

- The broader historical suite covers adapters, Predict and streaming, not every repository test. The three skips and eleven existing deprecation warnings remain reported rather than counted as passes.
- Multi-branch scalar unions retain their existing behavior; this is not a general union repair. For example, separate `Literal[1] | Literal[2]` branches still reject nested text `1`, as on the baseline.
- Untyped/Any representation is unchanged; there is no lossless-untyped claim. This does not duplicate #10761's untyped list policy or #10789/#10755's prompt metadata work. No changes to generation, provider behavior or model quality are claimed.
- Local validation used offline recording engines. Historical exact-head CI completed with 25 successful checks and one expected skipped publish job; Greptile reached 5/5 after the compatibility correction. Those are recorded gates, not a new CI run caused by this description edit.

AI disclosure: maintainer-directed release robustness investigation, implemented with Amp. Prompt: “Own R3 nested numeric/bool Literals; recheck latest main, prove fail-before/pass-after through public APIs, keep the fix small, and run independent review.”

title: fix: preserve CoT reasoning in Refine feedback
body:
## Refine discards the reasoning it needs to critique a failed attempt

`Refine` runs a program, scores its answer, and asks a feedback predictor for advice before retrying a low-scoring attempt. When that program is `ChainOfThought`, the feedback should include both its answer and the available reasoning that produced it.

Instead, default CoT reasoning becomes `<non-serializable: Reasoning>` in **both `program_trajectory` and `program_outputs`**. The feedback predictor loses the explanation of the mistake even though the original prediction contains it. This affects native thinking summaries and the explicit fallback plan; callers using `rationale_field_type=str` are unaffected.

For the reproduction below, the decisive difference in each feedback structure is:

```diff
- "reasoning": "<non-serializable: Reasoning>"
+ "reasoning": "I subtracted the 10 percent discount as $10 from the $240 subtotal."
```

This is silent information loss, not a general Refine crash. The deterministic reproduction returns the successful second answer even before the fix; what fails is the assertion that the feedback request retained the failed attempt's reasoning. The test does **not** claim that preserving reasoning guarantees a better answer from a real model.

## Why the text is lost, and why this fixes it

In `Refine.forward`, `dict(o)` and `dict(outputs)` expose the prediction fields but leave the nested `dspy.Reasoning` objects intact. Before sending those structures to `OfferFeedback`, Refine calls `recursive_mask` and then JSON-encodes the result.

`recursive_mask` first tries `orjson.dumps`. `dspy.Reasoning` has a string representation, but is not itself a JSON string, so that attempt raises `TypeError`. Existing recursion handles dictionaries, lists, and tuples; any other unsupported object becomes a placeholder. That fallback discards valid reasoning text.

The production change is three added lines in `dspy/predict/refine.py`, immediately after the failed serialization attempt and before container recursion:

```diff
     except TypeError:
         pass
 
+    if isinstance(o, dspy.Reasoning):
+        return str(o)
+
     # If it's a dictionary, apply recursively to its values.
```

The existing recursion now preserves reasoning wherever it occurs in the trajectory or final outputs. The conversion uses `Reasoning`'s existing string-content contract. Other unsupported objects remain masked, and already-serializable values retain their behavior. This belongs in Refine's feedback serialization: it changes neither CoT reasoning generation nor provider reasoning controls, and is separate from #10615.

## Historical implementation evidence

The implementation run used baseline main [afaac264](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b) and the patch committed as PR head [c5977bec](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/c5977bec922059c54776ffff25b9e0be68b286d8). These are recorded execution results from the original committed regression test, not executions of the revised invoice example below.

**Before:** copy the original committed regression test onto baseline main, without changing production code:

```console
$ .venv/bin/pytest tests/predict/test_refine.py -k preserves -q --tb=short
FAILED tests/predict/test_refine.py::test_refine_feedback_preserves_reasoning[Reasoning-False]
FAILED tests/predict/test_refine.py::test_refine_feedback_preserves_reasoning[Reasoning-True]
2 failed, 2 passed, 3 deselected in 0.75s
```

**After:** apply the conversion and run the full Refine, CoT, and MultiChainComparison test files, including all four regression cases:

```console
$ .venv/bin/pytest tests/predict/test_refine.py tests/predict/test_chain_of_thought.py tests/predict/test_multi_chain_comparison.py -q
73 passed, 7 warnings in 1.06s
```

The warnings are existing `InputField`/`OutputField` `prefix` deprecations in MultiChainComparison tests.

| Reasoning type | Engine / reasoning path | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `dspy.Reasoning` (CoT default) | Non-native; explicit fallback plan | Fail | Pass |
| `dspy.Reasoning` (CoT default) | Native thinking | Fail | Pass |
| `str` | Non-native; explicit text | Pass | Pass |
| `str` | Native-capable engine; explicit string control | Pass | Pass |

The historical tests checked a scripted successful second answer, exactly one feedback request, and two copies of the failed explanation in that request—one in the trajectory and one in the program outputs. The revised example below preserves those controls with an invoice calculation and an independent arithmetic reward.

## Complete offline reproduction: validate a discounted invoice

A finance assistant computes the total for three items at $80 each with a 10% discount. A plausible first mistake treats the percentage as a flat $10 reduction, returning $230 instead of $216. `Refine` uses an independently calculated monetary reward, rejects that attempt, and asks for feedback. The feedback must retain the explanation of the mistaken discount, not just the wrong total.

This is a runnable scenario adaptation, not the original committed test verbatim. It drives real `ChainOfThought`, `Refine`, adapter processing, and public LM request/response types through a **caller-owned deterministic engine**. The engine scripts both attempts and the advice; it does not infer the correction from the feedback. A successful second total therefore proves neither model quality nor that feedback improved the answer. The regression assertion checks that the first attempt's available explanation actually reaches the feedback request in both structures. No DSPy internals are patched and no provider calls or credentials are needed. ChatAdapter is explicit, with JSON fallback disabled.

Save this as `test_refine_reasoning_repro.py` in a DSPy checkout. Use a file rather than stdin or a REPL because Refine inspects the reward function's source.

```python
from decimal import Decimal

import pytest
import dspy
from dspy.lm15 import Message, Response, TextPart, ThinkingPart, Usage


class InvoiceTotal(dspy.Signature):
    """Calculate the invoice total after the percentage discount, before tax."""
    quantity: int = dspy.InputField()
    unit_price: str = dspy.InputField(desc="USD per item")
    discount_percent: str = dspy.InputField()
    total: str = dspy.OutputField(desc="USD, with two decimal places")


def invoice_reward(inputs, prediction):
    subtotal = Decimal(inputs["quantity"]) * Decimal(inputs["unit_price"])
    expected = (subtotal * (1 - Decimal(inputs["discount_percent"]) / 100)).quantize(Decimal("0.01"))
    return float(Decimal(prediction.total) == expected)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("native", [False, True])
@pytest.mark.parametrize("reasoning_type", [dspy.Reasoning, str])
def test_invoice_feedback_preserves_mistaken_discount(native, reasoning_type):
    feedback = []
    mistaken = "I subtracted the 10 percent discount as $10 from the $240 subtotal."
    attempts = iter([
        ("230.00", mistaken),
        ("216.00", "Three items cost $240; a 10 percent discount removes $24."),
    ])
    observed_rewards = []

    def reward(inputs, prediction):
        score = invoice_reward(inputs, prediction)
        observed_rewards.append(score)
        return score

    class Engine:
        supports_reasoning = native

        def complete(self, request):
            if "program_trajectory" in request.system:
                feedback.append("\n".join(message.text for message in request.messages))
                text = (
                    '[[ ## discussion ## ]]\nThe discount is a percentage, not a dollar amount.\n'
                    '[[ ## advice ## ]]\n{"predict": "Multiply the subtotal by 1 minus discount_percent / 100."}'
                )
                parts = []
            else:
                total, reasoning = next(attempts)
                name = "plan" if "[[ ## plan ## ]]" in request.system else "reasoning"
                text = f"[[ ## {name} ## ]]\n{reasoning}\n" if f"[[ ## {name} ## ]]" in request.system else ""
                text += f"[[ ## total ## ]]\n{total}"
                parts = [ThinkingPart(reasoning)] if native else []
            return Response(None, request.model, Message.assistant(parts + [TextPart(text)]), "stop", Usage())

    cot = dspy.ChainOfThought(InvoiceTotal, rationale_field_type=reasoning_type)
    lm = dspy.LM("custom/invoice-review", engine=Engine(), cache=False)
    with dspy.context(lm=lm, adapter=dspy.ChatAdapter(use_json_adapter_fallback=False)):
        result = dspy.Refine(cot, N=2, reward_fn=reward, threshold=1)(
            quantity=3, unit_price="80.00", discount_percent="10"
        )
    assert result.total == "216.00"
    assert observed_rewards == [0.0, 1.0]
    assert len(feedback) == 1
    # Both the trace and final program output must retain the failed reasoning.
    assert feedback[0].count(mistaken) == 2
```

Normalized reproduction command with the checkout's installed development environment:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m pytest test_refine_reasoning_repro.py -q --tb=short
```

### Fresh execution of the exact invoice snippet

The inline Python block above was extracted unchanged and executed with `-q --tb=short` against isolated exports of baseline [afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/afaac26465663293d2cac64e71add28232e81e8b) and fixed head [c5977bec922059c54776ffff25b9e0be68b286d8](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/c5977bec922059c54776ffff25b9e0be68b286d8). The imported `dspy` path was checked before each run; the installed dependency environment was shared, and no source files were changed. These are new scenario executions, separate from the historical 73-test run above.

Baseline output excerpt:

```text
assert feedback[0].count(mistaken) == 2
E   assert 0 == 2
FAILED test_refine_reasoning_repro.py::test_invoice_feedback_preserves_mistaken_discount[Reasoning-False]
FAILED test_refine_reasoning_repro.py::test_invoice_feedback_preserves_mistaken_discount[Reasoning-True]
2 failed, 2 passed in 0.46s
```

Fixed-head result:

```text
4 passed in 0.46s
```

All four cases reach the scripted $216 total and reward sequence `[0.0, 1.0]` on both revisions. Only the two default-Reasoning cases lose the failed explanation before the fix; legacy string reasoning retains it. The corrected cases preserve the explanation twice in the actual feedback request. The source of the explanation is the failed LM response, not the task input or reward function.

The original committed regression test remains available separately:

```bash
uv run pytest tests/predict/test_refine.py -k preserves_reasoning -q
```

## Additional validation and limits

- The original independent public-API probe also passed after the fix: **4 passed, 74 deselected in 0.64s**.
- `ruff check dspy/predict/refine.py tests/predict/test_refine.py`, `uv run --locked --extra dev ty check`, pre-commit on both changed files, and `git diff --check` passed.
- An independent read-only review found no findings or blockers. That reviewer did not rerun the tests; runtime evidence is from the implementation run above.
- Historical investigation attributed the default-path regression to #10643. The direct before/after evidence here is against the explicitly named main baseline, not a fresh bisect of that introducing PR.
- This preserves available reasoning text. It does not recover provider-omitted reasoning, measure feedback quality or optimizer convergence, or add serialization for arbitrary Pydantic models. Local suite counts above are focused coverage, not a claim of a full-repository local run.

One small fix PR per independent finding; no merges.”

title: feat(flex): graduate dspy.Flex from experimental
body:
## Problem
Isaac approved Flex graduation for DSPy 3.5 (CMP-1291), but its decorator and docs still designate it experimental. Follows merged RLM graduation #10835 and the ReAct docs precedent #10795.

## Change
Remove Flex's `@experimental` and unused import, the API warning, the deep-dive instability section, and the variants-page label. Preserve `dspy.Flex`, `dspy.predict.flex.Flex`, and `dspy.predict.flex.flex.Flex`; no new aliases or import migration. Keep interpreter/security/persistence caveats.

## Proof
- Public import/designation regression fails on unchanged main's experimental notice and passes here.
- Credential-free `pytest tests/flex tests/utils/test_annotation.py tests/predict/test_rlm.py::TestRLMInitialization -q --deno -n 4 -p no:cacheprovider`: **241 passed** (including real Deno/Pyodide, DummyLM only).
- Production AST is identical after removing just the experimental import/decorator; the decorator only changes the docstring.
- Changed-file Ruff, `uv run --locked --extra dev ty check`, pre-commit and `git diff --check` pass. Simplicity audit: minimal at the designation owner, no new machinery.
- Full current docs build (`python docs/scripts/build_docs.py current --config docs/mkdocs.yml --output /tmp/flex-grad-site`) passes with six unrelated existing link warnings.
- Published head [12620fea](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/commit/12620fea14cfd73014fc33883c331924753c9f83): 25 successful checks / 1 publishing skip; [CI](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/actions/runs/42648517006) and [docs](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/actions/runs/42648517008) succeed; [head-matched Greptile 5/5](https://github.com/stanfordnlp/dspy/pull/10836#issuecomment-6744475553).
- [Independent narrow-diff review](https://ampcode.com/artifacts/dspy-3-5-exact-head-review-and-maintenance-a49b9fa5-b2d9-458e-b452-1899ba391602): no blockers or required simplification; isolated fetched-head binding/annotation suite `--deno`: **24 passed, 0 skipped**, with independent base-fail/head-pass import/notice controls and AST equivalence. Rendered API, deep dive and variants pages checked; interpreter/security caveats remain.

## Limits
Designation/docs only: no runtime, constructor, sync/async, optimizer, transport, serialization or security changes. No paid local model calls or new quality/performance claims. Existing Ledgerly evidence in #10790 (author-reported 20/20 held-out, 10/10 Pyodide) is context already recorded in CMP-1291, not independently rerun here; that PR's extra APIs are not included. No merge authorized.

## Release note
